title: Statistical Tests and Analysis
text:
This section covers common statistical tests used in medical research, implemented in R.



# Load necessary libraries
library(tidyverse)

── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
✔ ggplot2   4.0.4     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
✔ purrr     1.2.2     
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors

library(gtsummary)

# Example data (simulated; the seed makes the numbers the same on every render)
set.seed(2026)
data <- data.frame(
  age = rnorm(100, 50, 10),
  blood_pressure = rnorm(100, 120, 15),
  treatment = sample(c("A", "B"), 100, replace = TRUE)
)

# Summary statistics
data %>% 
  tbl_summary()











Characteristic
N = 1001




age
48 (42, 56)


blood_pressure
123 (111, 131)


treatment




    A
49 (49%)


    B
51 (51%)



1 Median (Q1, Q3); n (%)














# Two-sample t-test
t.test(blood_pressure ~ treatment, data = data)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  blood_pressure by treatment
t = 1.0107, df = 96.367, p-value = 0.3147
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group A and group B is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -2.804691  8.624570
sample estimates:
mean in group A mean in group B 
       123.3066        120.3966 






# Create categorical data
data$outcome <- sample(c("Improved", "Not Improved"), 100, replace = TRUE)

# Chi-square test
chisq.test(table(data$treatment, data$outcome))


    Pearson's Chi-squared test with Yates' continuity correction

data:  table(data$treatment, data$outcome)
X-squared = 1.0283, df = 1, p-value = 0.3106













Outcome
Groups / predictor
Usual test




Continuous
2 independent groups
Two-sample (Welch) t-test


Continuous
same people measured twice (before/after)
Paired t-test


Continuous, skewed or small sample
2 independent groups
Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann-Whitney)


Continuous
3 or more groups
One-way ANOVA (Kruskal-Wallis if skewed)


Categorical (yes/no)
categorical
Chi-square test (Fisher’s exact if expected counts are small)







t.test(blood_pressure ~ treatment, data = data)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  blood_pressure by treatment
t = 1.0107, df = 96.367, p-value = 0.3147
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group A and group B is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -2.804691  8.624570
sample estimates:
mean in group A mean in group B 
       123.3066        120.3966 



R uses Welch’s t-test by default (does not assume equal variances).
The confidence interval is for the first group minus the second (A − B), so the sign follows the order of the groups.
The sample estimates show each group’s mean.





# paired: the same 30 people before and after
before <- rnorm(30, 140, 12)
after  <- before - rnorm(30, 5, 6)
t.test(before, after, paired = TRUE)


    Paired t-test

data:  before and after
t = 5.3735, df = 29, p-value = 8.985e-06
alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 3.020140 6.731862
sample estimates:
mean difference 
       4.876001 

# non-parametric alternative for two independent groups
wilcox.test(blood_pressure ~ treatment, data = data)


    Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction

data:  blood_pressure by treatment
W = 1360, p-value = 0.4482
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0






A p-value says how surprising the data would be if there were no true difference.
It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and not the probability the result is “due to chance”.
It says nothing about the size or importance of the difference: look at the estimate and its confidence interval.
A large p-value is weak evidence against “no difference”. It is not proof that there is none.





Regression modeling now has its own dedicated module — see Regression Analysis for simple/multiple regression, diagnostics, and logistic regression.

title: Statistical Tests and Analysis
text:
Self-check quiz

Mean systolic BP is compared between two independent groups of 60 patients each. Which test is the usual first choice?

A chi-square test of the two groups
A paired t-test
A two-sample (Welch) t-test
A correlation test



The same 30 patients have their BP measured before and after a treatment. Which test fits?

A paired t-test
A two-sample t-test
A chi-square test
A one-way ANOVA



A study reports p = 0.03. Which statement is correct?

There is a 3% probability that there is no real difference at all
The difference is large enough to matter clinically
Such data would be unusual if there were no real difference
The result has a 97% chance of being repeated



A trial finds p = 0.40 for a difference in BP. What can you conclude?

The treatments have now been shown to be equal
The data give weak evidence of a difference
The trial must contain a calculation error
The difference is 40% of the control mean



Two categorical variables (smoker yes/no, hypertension yes/no) are compared. Which test fits, with large expected counts?

A two-sample t-test
A Wilcoxon rank-sum test
A one-way ANOVA
A chi-square test

These examples show the R workflow for medical data: import, clean, summarize, test, and visualize.




Real datasets often need the same test or summary repeated across many variables. Loops (and their apply/purrr equivalents) let you do that without copy-pasting code.



vars <- c("age_of_participants", "sbp_in_mm_hg", "dbp_in_mm_hg")

for (v in vars) {
  cat("Summary of", v, ":\n")
  print(summary(p[[v]]))
  cat("\n")
}

Summary of age_of_participants :
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  18.00   29.00   42.00   43.85   58.00   95.00 

Summary of sbp_in_mm_hg :
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   83.0   108.0   120.0   120.8   130.5   199.0 

Summary of dbp_in_mm_hg :
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  52.00   86.00  108.00   97.31  108.00  125.00 





For simple per-column operations the apply family avoids manual bookkeeping:

# Same variables as the for-loop above, without the explicit loop
sapply(p[vars], mean, na.rm = TRUE)

age_of_participants        sbp_in_mm_hg        dbp_in_mm_hg 
           43.84786           120.75911            97.30586 


Use a for loop when each iteration has side effects (printing, saving files, building up a report) or when the logic is easier to follow step-by-step; reach for sapply() when you just need one result per element.

title: Data Analysis
text:
Self-check quiz

Foot pain was recorded before and after an intervention in the same people. Which test compares the two proportions?

Chi-square test for association
McNemar’s chi-square test
Chi-square goodness-of-fit
Two-sample t-test



chisq.test(x = observed, p = c(0.5, 0.5)) on screened yes/no tests what?

Whether screening is associated with sex
Whether screening differs from a 50:50 split
Whether screening changed between two visits
Whether the screening counts are normal



Points on a Q-Q plot bend away from the line at both ends. What does that suggest?

The sample mean has been computed the wrong way
The two variables are strongly correlated
The tails differ from a normal distribution
The data have no missing values in them


Your score:  (first attempt counts)

title: Merged Visuals
text:
One plot type rarely tells the whole story. Merged visuals layer two views of the same data so the reader sees, for example, the shape of a distribution and every individual value. Three ways to merge:
The rule for every merged plot: each layer must answer a question the other cannot. If a layer only decorates, drop it.
library(tidyverse); library(patchwork); library(ggridges); library(ggside)
ncd <- read_csv("../data/ncd_survey.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(phys_act = factor(phys_act, levels = c("low", "moderate", "high")),
         htn = factor(htn, 0:1, c("No hypertension", "Hypertension")))
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))

title: Merged Visuals
text:
Categorical: bar chart + labels

edu <- ncd |> count(education) |> mutate(pct = n / sum(n))
ggplot(edu, aes(x = fct_reorder(education, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#3498db") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(n, " (", scales::percent(pct, 1), ")")), vjust = -0.4) +
  labs(x = "Education", y = "Adults", title = "Education of the 600 adults") +
  expand_limits(y = max(edu$n) * 1.1)








The labels give the exact numbers, the bars the comparison. Missing education (NA) stays visible as its own bar.

title: Merged Visuals
text:
Continuous: histogram + density

ggplot(ncd, aes(x = sbp)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 5, fill = "grey80", colour = "white") +
  geom_density(colour = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 140, linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", y = "Density", title = "Systolic BP: bins and a smooth curve")








after_stat(density) puts the histogram on the density scale, so both layers share the y-axis. The dashed line marks the hypertension threshold.

title: Merged Visuals
text:
Continuous by group: ridgelines

ggplot(ncd, aes(x = sbp, y = phys_act, fill = phys_act)) +
  geom_density_ridges(alpha = 0.7, quantile_lines = TRUE, quantiles = 2) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", y = "Physical activity", title = "Distributions side by side, medians marked")








Ridgelines compare many distributions in little space; quantile_lines adds the median of each.

title: Merged Visuals
section: Category vs category: grouped bars + facets
text:
Category vs category: grouped bars + facets

ncd |> count(residence, tobacco, htn) |>
  group_by(residence, tobacco) |> mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) |> ungroup() |>
  filter(htn == "Hypertension") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tobacco, y = pct, fill = tobacco)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(pct, 1)), vjust = -0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ residence) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.6)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(No = "grey60", Yes = "#e74c3c"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Tobacco use", y = "Adults with hypertension", title = "Hypertension by tobacco use, within residence")








The facets hold residence fixed, so each panel compares tobacco users with non-users in the same setting.

title: Merged Visuals
section: Continuous vs continuous: scatter + marginal histograms
text:
Continuous vs continuous: scatter + marginal histograms

ggplot(ncd, aes(x = bmi, y = sbp)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "#e74c3c") +
  geom_xsidehistogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "grey70") +
  geom_ysidehistogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "grey70") +
  theme(ggside.panel.scale = 0.2) +
  labs(x = "BMI (kg/m²)", y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", title = "The relationship and each variable's distribution")








The margins show that BMI is roughly symmetric and SBP slightly right-skewed: information the cloud of points hides.

title: Merged Visuals
text:
Bubble chart + trend line

villages <- ncd |> group_by(village) |>
  summarise(bmi = mean(bmi, na.rm = TRUE), sbp = mean(sbp), n = n())
ggplot(villages, aes(x = bmi, y = sbp)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n), alpha = 0.5, colour = "#2c3e50") +
  geom_smooth(aes(weight = n), method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "#e74c3c") +
  labs(x = "Village mean BMI", y = "Village mean systolic BP", size = "Adults", title = "Villages: means, sizes and a weighted trend")








Each bubble is a village, not a person: a trend between village means is an ecological association and need not hold for individuals.

title: Merged Visuals
section: Category vs continuous: box + points, violin + box
text:
Category vs continuous: box + points, violin + box

p1 <- ggplot(ncd, aes(phys_act, sbp)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.25) +
  labs(x = "Physical activity", y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", title = "Box + every adult")
p2 <- ggplot(ncd, aes(phys_act, sbp)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "grey85") +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA) +
  labs(x = "Physical activity", y = NULL, title = "Violin + box")
p1 + p2








Points show how many people stand behind each box; a violin shows the shape. outlier.shape = NA avoids drawing outliers twice.

title: Merged Visuals
text:
Time series: line + area

dengue <- read_csv("../data/dengue_wards.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  group_by(year, month) |> summarise(cases = sum(cases), rain = mean(rain_mm), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(sprintf("%d-%02d-01", year, month)))
k <- max(dengue$cases) / max(dengue$rain)          # put rain on the cases scale
ggplot(dengue, aes(date)) +
  geom_area(aes(y = rain * k), fill = "#3498db", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = cases), colour = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous("Dengue cases (all wards)", sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . / k, name = "Mean rainfall (mm)")) +
  labs(x = NULL, title = "Cases follow the rains by about a month")








A second axis is acceptable only when both series are clearly labelled and the scaling is stated; otherwise use two panels.

title: Merged Visuals
section: Map: choropleth + bubbles, with an inset zoom
text:
Map: choropleth + bubbles, with an inset zoom

library(sf)
blocks <- st_read("../data/gis/district_blocks.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
centres <- st_centroid(blocks)
main <- ggplot(blocks) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = dengue_per_100k), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = centres, aes(size = dengue_cases), shape = 21, fill = NA, colour = "black") +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "OrRd", direction = 1, name = "Per 100,000") +
  labs(size = "Cases", title = "Rate (colour) and count (circle) together") +
  theme_void()
box <- st_bbox(blocks); zoom <- c(xmin = box[["xmax"]] - (box[["xmax"]] - box[["xmin"]]) / 3, ymax = box[["ymin"]] + (box[["ymax"]] - box[["ymin"]]) / 3)
inset <- ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = dengue_per_100k), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "OrRd", direction = 1, guide = "none") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(zoom[["xmin"]], box[["xmax"]]), ylim = c(box[["ymin"]], zoom[["ymax"]])) +
  theme_void() + theme(panel.border = element_rect(fill = NA))
main <- main + annotate("rect", xmin = zoom[["xmin"]], xmax = box[["xmax"]], ymin = box[["ymin"]], ymax = zoom[["ymax"]],
                        fill = NA, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.8)            # where the zoom comes from
main + (inset + labs(title = "Zoom: south-east")) + plot_layout(widths = c(3, 1))








Colour shows the rate (fair comparison between blocks of different size); circles show the count (where the work is). The second panel enlarges the south-east corner (the rectangle), where the high rates cluster.

When it helps
Watch out




Labels on bars
exact values matter
clutter with many bars

title: Iteration: Doing the Same Thing Many Times
text:
Medical analyses repeat: the same summary for 12 variables, the same test for 5 outcomes, the same plot for each district. Copy-pasting code 12 times is how mistakes get in (one copy keeps an old variable name). This page shows four safer ways, from simplest to most general. Data: the NCD survey (data/ncd_survey.csv).

library(tidyverse)
ncd <- read_csv(c("../data/ncd_survey.csv", "data/ncd_survey.csv")[file.exists(c("../data/ncd_survey.csv", "data/ncd_survey.csv"))][1], show_col_types = FALSE)




ncd |> summarise(across(c(sbp, dbp, bmi), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)))

# A tibble: 1 × 3
    sbp   dbp   bmi
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1  132.  59.7  23.0



across(columns, function) applies the function to each column inside summarise() or mutate().
\(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE) is a small unnamed function; x stands for “the column”.
Pick columns by name, c(a, b), or by type, where(is.numeric).
Several functions at once, with names:


ncd |> summarise(across(c(sbp, bmi), list(mean = \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), sd = \(x) sd(x, na.rm = TRUE))))

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  sbp_mean sbp_sd bmi_mean bmi_sd
     <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl>
1     132.   16.8     23.0   3.58



ncd |> mutate(across(c(sbp, dbp), \(x) x / 10)) |> select(sbp, dbp) |> head(3)    # the same change to two columns

# A tibble: 3 × 2
    sbp   dbp
  <dbl> <dbl>
1  13.1   5.7
2  13.5   6.1
3  12.7   5.7






for (v in c("sbp", "dbp", "bmi")) {
  cat(v, ": mean", round(mean(ncd[[v]], na.rm = TRUE), 1), "\n")
}

sbp : mean 132.3 
dbp : mean 59.7 
bmi : mean 23 



for (v in <items>) { <what to do> } runs the block once for each item, and v holds the current item.
ncd[[v]] picks the column whose name is stored in v (ncd$v would look for a column called “v”).
A loop prints or stores results; it only shows output if you ask (print(), cat()).
A loop that adds up:


total <- 0
for (i in 1:4) total <- total + i
total

[1] 10






sapply(ncd[c("sbp", "dbp", "bmi")], mean, na.rm = TRUE)       # a named vector of means

      sbp       dbp       bmi 
132.28500  59.68833  22.95258 



# one t-test per outcome, results kept in a tidy table
outcomes <- c("sbp", "dbp", "bmi")
map_dfr(outcomes, \(y) {
  t <- t.test(reformulate("sex", y), data = ncd)
  tibble(outcome = y, difference = unname(diff(rev(t$estimate))), p = t$p.value)
})

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  outcome difference       p
  <chr>        <dbl>   <dbl>
1 sbp         -3.78  0.00595
2 dbp         -1.61  0.0385 
3 bmi          0.387 0.193  



map() / sapply() return one result per item, collected for you: no empty vector to grow by hand.
reformulate("sex", y) builds the formula y ~ sex from text, so the loop can change the outcome.
map_dfr() stacks tibbles into one table; map_dbl() returns numbers.





pct_above <- function(x, cut) {
  mean(x >= cut, na.rm = TRUE) * 100      # the last value is returned
}
pct_above(ncd$sbp, 140)

[1] 32

pct_above(ncd$bmi, 30)

[1] 2.405498



A function has arguments (x, cut), a body in { }, and returns its last expression.
Write one when you copy the same 3 or more lines twice. Name it for what it does.
Test it on a case where you know the answer: pct_above(c(1, 5, 10, 20), 10) should be 50.










Warning




Growing a vector inside a loop (res <- c(res, new)) is slow and error-prone; use sapply() / map().
Forgetting na.rm = TRUE inside the function you repeat: one NA turns every result into NA.
ncd$v vs ncd[[v]]: with the variable name in v, use [[ ]].
Overwriting the original data in a loop; save results to a new object.
Many tests at once means many p-values: see multiple testing on the Statistical Tests page.

  mutate(

      sys_bp_0m < 120 & dia_bp_0m < 80 ~ "Normal",

      (sys_bp_0m >= 130 & sys_bp_0m < 140) |

Binary outcomes
Single condition
Simpler syntax

case_when()

Multiple outcomes

  condition2 ~ value2,
  TRUE ~ default_value
)

title: Data Wrangling in R
text:
Why lubridate?

Dates are complex (leap years, time zones, daylight savings)
lubridate makes date operations intuitive
Part of tidyverse but must be loaded separately
Essential for healthcare data with visit dates, follow-ups

text:
Age Calculation from Dates

Question: Calculate age from birthdate




Show the code
# Example with made-up birthdates
example_data <- tibble(
  patient_id = 1:3,
  birthdate = ymd(c("1980-05-15", "1965-12-20", "1990-03-08")),
  visit_date = ymd(c("2024-01-15", "2024-01-15", "2024-01-15"))
)

example_data |> 
  mutate(
    age_years = interval(birthdate, visit_date) / years(1),
    age_months = interval(birthdate, visit_date) / months(1)
  )


#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   patient_id birthdate  visit_date age_years age_months
#>        <int> <date>     <date>         <dbl>      <dbl>

#> 2          2 1965-12-20 2024-01-15      58.1       697.
#> 3          3 1990-03-08 2024-01-15      33.9       406.

# Load required packages
library(readxl)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(sf)          # For spatial data
library(maps)        # For map data
library(viridis)     # For color scales

# Load dataset
health_data <- read_excel("../../data/PublicHealth_BP_Dataset.xlsx")

# Aggregate data by region
region_summary <- health_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(Region)) %>%
  group_by(Region) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_bp = mean(SysBP_0m, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_cholesterol = mean(Cholesterol, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_bmi = mean(BMI, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_patients = n(),
    hypertension_rate = mean(SysBP_0m >= 140, na.rm = TRUE) * 100
  )

# Create theme
theme_map <- function() {
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = "serif", size = 12),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, hjust = 0.5),
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.title = element_text(size = 10),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "aliceblue")
  )
}

Choropleth Map - Code

Purpose: Show values across geographic regions using color
Goal: 🟣 Geographic + 🟢 Ranking


Code
# Get US state map data
us_states <- map_data("state")

# Create region to state mapping (simplified for demonstration)
region_states <- data.frame(
  region_name = c("North", "South", "East", "West"),
  states = c("new york,pennsylvania,ohio,michigan",
            "texas,florida,georgia,alabama",
            "massachusetts,connecticut,rhode island,maine",
            "california,oregon,washington,nevada")
)

# Expand and join
state_regions <- region_states %>%
  separate_rows(states, sep = ",") %>%
  rename(region_lower = states)

# Join with map data
map_data_full <- us_states %>%
  left_join(state_regions, by = c("region" = "region_lower")) %>%
  left_join(region_summary, by = c("region_name" = "Region"))

# Create choropleth map
ggplot(map_data_full, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = mean_bp)) +
  geom_polygon(color = "white", size = 0.3) +
  coord_map("albers", lat0 = 39, lat1 = 45) +  # Albers projection
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option = "plasma",
    name = "Mean Systolic BP\n(mmHg)",
    na.value = "gray90",
    guide = guide_colorbar(
      barwidth = 1.5,
      barheight = 15,
      title.position = "top"
    )
  ) +
  labs(title = "Average Blood Pressure by Region",
       subtitle = "Darker colors indicate higher blood pressure",
       caption = "Data: PublicHealth BP Dataset") +
  theme_map()

Point/Bubble Map - Code

Purpose: Show individual locations with value-sized markers
Goal: 🟣 Geographic + 🟡 Distribution


Code
# Create sample patient locations (simulated for demonstration)
set.seed(123)
patient_locations <- health_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(Region), !is.na(SysBP_0m)) %>%
  mutate(
    # Simulate coordinates within regions
    lat = case_when(
      Region == "North" ~ runif(n(), 40, 45),
      Region == "South" ~ runif(n(), 30, 35),
      Region == "East" ~ runif(n(), 39, 43),
      Region == "West" ~ runif(n(), 35, 42)
    ),
    lon = case_when(
      Region == "North" ~ runif(n(), -85, -75),
      Region == "South" ~ runif(n(), -100, -80),
      Region == "East" ~ runif(n(), -75, -70),
      Region == "West" ~ runif(n(), -125, -115)
    ),
    hypertensive = ifelse(SysBP_0m >= 140, "Yes", "No")
  ) %>%
  sample_n(200)  # Sample for clarity

# Create point map
ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = us_states, 
               aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
               fill = "white", color = "gray70") +
  geom_point(data = patient_locations,
            aes(x = lon, y = lat, color = hypertensive, size = SysBP_0m),
            alpha = 0.6) +
  coord_map("albers", lat0 = 39, lat1 = 45) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("No" = "#00A087", "Yes" = "#DC0000"),
                    name = "Hypertensive") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(1, 6), name = "Systolic BP\n(mmHg)") +
  labs(title = "Patient Locations by Blood Pressure Status",
       subtitle = "Point size = BP value | Color = Hypertension status (≥140 mmHg)",
       caption = "Sample of 200 patients") +
  theme_map()

Setup Code


Code
# Load required packages
library(readxl)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(zoo)      # For moving averages
library(lubridate) # For date handling

# Load dataset and create time series data
health_data <- read_excel("../../data/PublicHealth_BP_Dataset.xlsx")

# Aggregate by time point
time_data <- health_data %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(SysBP_0m, SysBP_3m, SysBP_6m),
               names_to = "TimePoint",
               values_to = "SysBP") %>%
  mutate(Month = case_when(
    TimePoint == "SysBP_0m" ~ 0,
    TimePoint == "SysBP_3m" ~ 3,
    TimePoint == "SysBP_6m" ~ 6
  ))

# Create theme
theme_custom <- function() {
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = "serif", size = 12),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, hjust = 0.5),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
}

text:
Smoothed Trend with LOESS - Code

Purpose: Show underlying trend while reducing noise
Goal: 🔵 Evolution


Code
# Calculate mean BP by treatment group over time
trend_data <- time_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(TreatmentGroup), !is.na(SysBP)) %>%
  group_by(TreatmentGroup, Month) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_bp = mean(SysBP, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_bp = sd(SysBP, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Create smoothed trend plot
ggplot(trend_data, aes(x = Month, y = mean_bp, 
                      color = TreatmentGroup, fill = TreatmentGroup)) +
  # Raw data points
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.6) +
  # Smoothed trend line
  geom_smooth(method = "loess",     # Locally weighted smoothing
              span = 0.75,          # Smoothness (larger = smoother)
              alpha = 0.2) +        # Confidence band transparency
  labs(title = "Blood Pressure Trends by Treatment Group",
       subtitle = "Smoothed LOESS curves with 95% confidence bands",
       x = "Time (months)",
       y = "Mean Systolic BP (mmHg)",
       color = "Treatment",
       fill = "Treatment") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 6, 12)) +
  theme_custom()

Area Chart with Confidence Bands - Code

Purpose: Emphasize magnitude and uncertainty over time
Goal: 🔵 Evolution + 🟡 Distribution


Code
# Calculate confidence intervals manually
trend_ci <- trend_data %>%
  mutate(
    lower = mean_bp - 1.96 * se_bp,  # 95% CI
    upper = mean_bp + 1.96 * se_bp
  )

# Create area chart with confidence band
ggplot(trend_ci, aes(x = Month, y = mean_bp, 
                    color = TreatmentGroup, fill = TreatmentGroup)) +
  # Confidence band as ribbon
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), 
              alpha = 0.3, color = NA) +
  # Mean line
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  # Points at measurement times
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Blood Pressure Changes with 95% Confidence Intervals",
       subtitle = "Shaded areas show uncertainty in estimates",
       x = "Time (months)",
       y = "Mean Systolic BP (mmHg)",
       color = "Treatment",
       fill = "Treatment") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 6, 12)) +
  theme_custom()

  # Line and points
  geom_line(color = "#4DBBD5", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(size = 4, color = "#4DBBD5") +
  # Annotate starting point
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 142, 
           label = "Baseline\n140 mmHg", 
           hjust = 0.5, vjust = -0.5, size = 4, fontface = "bold") +
  # Annotate 6-month check
  annotate("segment", x = 6, y = 125, xend = 6, yend = 130,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm")), 
           color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = 6, y = 123, 
           label = "First improvement\n-15 mmHg", 
           hjust = 0.5, size = 3.5, color = "red") +
  # Annotate final result
  annotate("text", x = 12, y = 118, 
           label = "Final: 120 mmHg\n✓ Target achieved", 
           hjust = 0.5, vjust = 1.2, size = 4, fontface = "bold", color = "darkgreen") +
  # Add horizontal reference line for target BP
  geom_hline(yintercept = 120, linetype = "dashed", 
             color = "darkgreen", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Treatment A: Blood Pressure Reduction Over 12 Months",
       subtitle = "Green line shows target BP of 120 mmHg",
       x = "Time (months)",
       y = "Mean Systolic BP (mmHg)") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 6, 12)) +
  ylim(110, 145) +
  theme_custom()

title: Time Series - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Effective Annotations

When to Annotate:

Key milestones - Important time points
Threshold crossings - When target is reached
Notable events - Interventions, policy changes
Unexpected changes - Spikes or drops
Comparisons - Differences from baseline

Best Practices:

Don’t over-annotate - 2-4 annotations max
Use arrows for clarity
Color-code meaningfully (red = bad, green = good)
Keep text brief - Key numbers + interpretation
Position carefully - Avoid overlapping

Small Multiples - Code

Purpose: Compare many series side-by-side
Goal: 🔵 Evolution + 🟢 Ranking


Code
# Create small multiples by region
region_trends <- time_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(Region), !is.na(SysBP)) %>%
  group_by(Region, Month) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_bp = mean(SysBP, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"

# Small multiples plot
ggplot(region_trends, aes(x = Month, y = mean_bp)) +
  geom_line(color = "#3C5488", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "#3C5488") +
  geom_area(fill = "#3C5488", alpha = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ Region, ncol = 2) +  # Split by region
  labs(title = "Blood Pressure Trends Across Regions",
       subtitle = "Small multiples enable direct comparison",
       x = "Time (months)",
       y = "Mean Systolic BP (mmHg)") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 6, 12)) +
  theme_custom() +
  theme(
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "gray90", color = "black"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    panel.spacing = unit(1.5, "lines")  # Space between panels

Interpreting Small Multiples

Power of Small Multiples:

Same scale enables direct comparison

Each region shows similar range

Pattern differences are immediately visible

West shows gradual increase
North shows decrease
East and South relatively stable

text:
Percent Change Plot - Code

Purpose: Show relative changes from baseline
Goal: 🔵 Evolution + comparison


Code
# Calculate percent change from baseline
pct_change_data <- time_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(TreatmentGroup), !is.na(SysBP)) %>%
  group_by(TreatmentGroup, Month) %>%
  summarise(mean_bp = mean(SysBP, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(TreatmentGroup) %>%
  mutate(
    baseline = first(mean_bp),           # Get baseline value
    pct_change = 100 * (mean_bp - baseline) / baseline  # % change
  )

# Create percent change plot
ggplot(pct_change_data, aes(x = Month, y = pct_change, 
                           color = TreatmentGroup, group = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_point(size = 3.5) +
  labs(title = "Percent Change in Blood Pressure from Baseline",
       subtitle = "Negative values indicate improvement",
       x = "Time (months)",
       y = "Change from Baseline (%)",
       color = "Treatment") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 6, 12)) +
  theme_custom()

title: Time Series - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Interpreting Percent Change

Why Use Percent Change?

Normalizes different baselines

Groups with different starting points comparable

Shows relative effect size

Treatment A: ~15% reduction
Treatment B: ~12% reduction
Control: ~0% change

Makes communication easier

“15% reduction” more intuitive than “20 mmHg decrease”

Useful for different scales

Can compare BP, cholesterol, weight, etc. on same plot


Limitation: Can mislead if baseline values are very small

title: Time Series - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Slope Graph - Code

Purpose: Highlight individual changes between two time points
Goal: 🔵 Evolution + individual patterns


Code
# Prepare data: baseline vs 12-month by treatment
slope_data <- health_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(TreatmentGroup), !is.na(SysBP_0m), !is.na(SysBP_6m)) %>%
  select(PatientID, TreatmentGroup, SysBP_0m, SysBP_6m) %>%
  group_by(TreatmentGroup) %>%
  slice_sample(n = 15) %>%  # Sample 15 patients per group
  ungroup() %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(SysBP_0m, SysBP_6m),
               names_to = "Time",
               values_to = "SysBP") %>%
  mutate(Time = ifelse(Time == "SysBP_0m", "Baseline", "6 Months"))

# Create slope graph
ggplot(slope_data, aes(x = Time, y = SysBP, group = PatientID,
                      color = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.6, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ TreatmentGroup, ncol = 3) +
  labs(title = "Individual Patient Blood Pressure Changes",
       subtitle = "Each line represents one patient (n=15 per group)",
       x = "",
       y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  theme_custom() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        strip.background = element_rect(fill = "gray90"),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))

Some up, some down (natural variation)

Individual variability is visible

Not all patients respond equally
Some non-responders in treatment groups

Response heterogeneity matters

Need to identify why some don’t respond


Advantage: Shows both group trend AND individual variation

Violin Plot - Code
🟡 Goal: Show full distribution shape by group


Code
# Create violin plot comparing BMI across regions
ggplot(data_clean, aes(x = Region, y = BMI, fill = Region)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.7, trim = FALSE) +  # Create violin shapes
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA) +  # Add boxplot inside

title: Continuous Plots - INTERMEDIATE
text:
How to Read Violin Plots
Using the previous plot:

OBSERVATION: - Median BMI: East 26.9, West 25.5, North 25.0, South 24.4 - West has the widest spread (SD 5.1), North the narrowest (SD 4.4) - Every region has a thin lower tail: a few BMI values near 11–12 - The bulk of each violin sits between about 22 and 30
INTERPRETATION: - BMI is similar across regions; East is about 2 units higher than South - The lower tails are implausible BMI values, visible in every region - A violin shows the tail that a box plot reduces to a few dots
IMPLICATIONS: - Check the very low BMI values before comparing regions - A difference of 2 units may matter clinically; test it, with region sizes of 40 to 65
ACTIONS: - Use violins when the shape matters (tails, two peaks); keep the inner box for the median and quartiles

Ridgeline Plot - Code

# Create ridgeline plot of Cholesterol by Exercise Frequency

ggplot(data_clean, aes(x = Cholesterol, y = ExerciseFreq, fill = ExerciseFreq)) +
  geom_density_ridges(alpha = 0.7, scale = 1.2) +  # Create overlapping densities
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", name = "Exercise Frequency") +
  labs(title = "Cholesterol Distribution by Exercise Frequency",
       x = "Cholesterol (mg/dL)",

Scatter with Regression Line - Code
⚫ Goal: Show correlation with statistical trend


Code
# Scatter plot with linear regression line and confidence interval
ggplot(data_clean, aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "steelblue", size = 2.5) +  # Add points
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "#E74C3C", 
              fill = "#E74C3C", alpha = 0.2, size = 1.2) +  # Add regression line + CI
  # Calculate and display correlation
  annotate("text", x = 25, y = 160, 
           label = paste("r =", round(cor(data_clean$Age, data_clean$SysBP_0m), 3)),
           family = "serif", size = 5, fontface = "bold") +
  labs(title = "Age vs. Baseline Systolic BP with Regression Line",
       subtitle = "Linear trend with 95% confidence interval",
       x = "Age (years)", 
       y = "Systolic Blood Pressure (mmHg)") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 12),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12))

text: Scatter with Regression - Plot

title: Continuous Plots - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Reading Advanced Continuous Plots
Using the regression plot:

OBSERVATION: - Correlation between age and baseline systolic BP: r = −0.09 (p = 0.22) - The regression line is almost flat (about −0.07 mmHg per year) - The confidence band is wide compared with the slope - Ages 18–79; systolic BP 110–159 mmHg
INTERPRETATION: - No evidence of a linear association between age and baseline BP in this sample - This is unusual: in most populations BP rises with age. With simulated data, or a small or selected sample, the expected pattern can be absent
IMPLICATIONS: - Do not draw a trend from a line that the data do not support: read the CI band and r together - Check how the sample was selected before generalising - A flat line here is a result, not an error in the plot

title: Continuous Plots - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Violin vs. Box Plot


Box Plot Shows: - 5-number summary - Median (50th percentile) - Quartiles (25th, 75th) - Outliers - Missing: Distribution shape
Use When: - Quick comparison needed - Focus on median/quartiles - Outliers are important

Violin Plot Shows: - Full distribution shape - Density at each value - Can see bimodal patterns - Shows skewness clearly - Missing: Exact quantiles
Use When: - Shape matters - Want to see multiple peaks - Comparing distributions - Publication quality needed

title: Continuous Plots - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Key Takeaways

Remember:

Violin plots show what box plots hide (distribution shape)
Ridgeline plots scale well to 5-10 groups
2D density reveals clustering patterns
Hexbin solves overplotting automatically
Always show confidence intervals on regression lines

Common Mistakes: - Using violin plots with < 20 observations per group - Too many groups in ridgeline (>10 gets cluttered) - Forgetting to show confidence intervals - Interpreting weak correlations as strong relationships - Not checking for non-linear patterns
Pro Tips: - Add boxplot inside violin for best of both worlds - scale parameter in ridgeline controls overlap - Use alpha transparency to show density overlaps - Always report correlation coefficient with regression

title: Category vs. Continuous - BASIC
section: What is Category vs. Continuous Data?
text:
What is Category vs. Continuous Data?


Definition:
Combining categorical variables (groups) with continuous variables (numeric measurements)

Compare numeric values across categories
Show distributions within groups
Analyze differences between segments


Examples in Our Dataset:

BMI by Gender
Blood Pressure by Treatment Group
Cholesterol by Region
Age by Smoking Status
Blood Sugar by Exercise Frequency

title: Category vs. Continuous - BASIC
text:
Analytical Goals

What questions can we answer?

🟡 Distribution - How do values spread within each category?
🟢 Ranking - Which group has highest/lowest values?
🔴 Part of Whole - How do groups contribute to total?
⚫ Correlation - Do patterns differ across groups?

Charts we’ll learn:

Box Plot
Grouped Bar Chart
Stacked Bar Chart

title: Category vs. Continuous - BASIC
text:
Setup: Load Data


Code

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# Load the dataset
data <- readxl::read_excel("../../data/PublicHealth_BP_Dataset.xlsx")

# Handle missing data for complete case analysis
data_clean <- data %>%
  filter(!is.na(ExerciseFreq), !is.na(ChronicDisease))  # Remove rows with missing values

title: Category vs. Continuous - BASIC
text:
Box Plot - Code
🟡 Goal: Compare distributions across groups


Code
# Create box plot comparing BMI by Treatment Group
ggplot(data_clean, aes(x = TreatmentGroup, y = BMI, fill = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.color = "red", outlier.size = 3) +  # Add box plots
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Control" = "#E74C3C", 
                                "Intervention" = "#3498DB"),
                    name = "Treatment Group") +  # Custom colors
  labs(title = "BMI Distribution by Treatment Group",
       x = "Treatment Group", y = "Body Mass Index (BMI)") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
        legend.position = "none")  # Hide legend (redundant with x-axis)



Box plot shows: minimum, Q1 (25%), median (50%), Q3 (75%), maximum, and outliers

title: Category vs. Continuous - BASIC
text: Box Plot - Plot

title: Category vs. Continuous - BASIC
text:
How to Read Box Plots
Using the previous plot:

Reading the 5-Number Summary (Control / Intervention): - Bottom whisker: lowest value within 1.5 × IQR of the box - Bottom of box (Q1): 25th percentile (22.4 / 23.0) - Line in box (Median): 50th percentile (24.6 / 25.8) - Top of box (Q3): 75th percentile (27.7 / 29.3) - Top whisker: highest value within 1.5 × IQR - Red dots: outliers beyond 1.5 × IQR (1 in Control, 2 in Intervention; the lowest BMI is 11.4)
OBSERVATION: - Median BMI 24.6 (Control) and 25.8 (Intervention) - Intervention box slightly taller (IQR 6.3 vs 5.4): a little more spread - Boxes largely overlap - A few very low BMI values appear as outliers
INTERPRETATION: - A difference of about 1 BMI unit between the groups at baseline; small next to the spread within each group - The groups look broadly comparable on BMI - The very low values (below 15) are implausible and should be checked
IMPLICATIONS: - A baseline difference this small is unlikely to confound a treatment comparison, but it can be adjusted for - Report the medians and IQRs in Table 1 - Decide what to do with implausible values before the analysis, and say so in the methods

title: Category vs. Continuous - BASIC
section: Box Plot with Multiple Categories - Code
text:
Box Plot with Multiple Categories - Code
🟡 Goal: Compare distributions across many groups


Code
# Compare Cholesterol across all regions
ggplot(data_clean, aes(x = reorder(Region, Cholesterol, FUN = median), 
                       y = Cholesterol, fill = Region)) +

title: Category vs. Continuous - BASIC
text:
Understanding Box Plots


The Box: - Bottom edge: Q1 (25th percentile) - Middle line: Median (50th percentile) - Top edge: Q3 (75th percentile) - Box height: IQR (Q3 - Q1)
The Whiskers: - Extend to 1.5 × IQR - Show data range (excluding outliers)

Outliers: - Points beyond whiskers - May indicate: - Data entry errors - Natural extreme values - Different population
Comparing Boxes: - Non-overlapping: likely different - Overlapping: may not be different - Check median positions - Compare IQR widths

title: Category vs. Continuous - BASIC
text:
Key Takeaways

Remember:

Box plots show distribution - not just means
Order categories - by median or logically
Grouped vs. Stacked bars - different purposes
Always show units - in axis labels
Handle outliers thoughtfully - investigate but don’t automatically remove

Common Mistakes:

Too many categories in one plot (>8)
Not ordering categories logically
Confusing grouped and stacked bars
Ignoring outliers without investigation
Comparing means without showing variation

title: Categorical Plots - BASIC
text:
What is Categorical Data?


Definition:
Data that represents categories, groups, or labels

Finite set of discrete values
No inherent numerical order (usually)
Qualitative rather than quantitative


Examples in Our Dataset:

Treatment Group (Control, Intervention)
Gender (Male, Female, Other)
Region (North, South, East, West)
Smoking Status
Alcohol Use
Exercise Frequency
Chronic Disease

title: Categorical Plots - BASIC
text:
Analytical Goals for Categorical Data

What questions can we answer?

🟢 Ranking - Which category is most/least common?
🟡 Distribution - How are observations spread across categories?
🔴 Part of Whole - What proportion does each category represent?

Charts we’ll learn:

Bar Chart (Vertical & Horizontal)
Pie Chart
Donut Chart
Stacked Bar Chart

title: Categorical Plots - BASIC
text:
How to Read Bar Charts
Using the previous plot as example:

OBSERVATION: - Non-smokers: 118 patients (largest group) - Former smokers: 43 patients - Current smokers: 37 patients (smallest group) - Clear ranking, with no group very small
INTERPRETATION: - 60% of participants are non-smokers - Current and former smokers together are 40% - Every smoking group has enough patients to describe
IMPLICATIONS: - Subgroups of smokers are still small (37 and 43): estimates within them will be imprecise - Non-smokers carry most of the weight of overall results - Consider stratified analysis by smoking status
ACTIONS: - Use smoking status as a stratification variable - Check statistical power before testing smoker subgroups - Watch for interaction effects with treatment

title: Categorical Plots - BASIC
text:
Pie Chart - Code
🔴 Goal: Part of a Whole


Code
# Calculate percentages for treatment groups
treatment_summary <- data_clean %>%
  count(TreatmentGroup) %>%
  mutate(percentage = n / sum(n) * 100)  # Calculate percentages

# Create pie chart using coord_polar transformation
ggplot(treatment_summary, aes(x = "", y = n, fill = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1, color = "white") +  # Create stacked bar
  coord_polar("y", start = 0) +  # Transform to polar coordinates (pie)
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Control" = "#E74C3C", "Intervention" = "#3498DB")) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(percentage, 1), "%")), 
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
            family = "serif", size = 5) +  # Add percentage labels
  labs(title = "Treatment Group Distribution",
       fill = "Group") +
  theme_void(base_family = "serif") +  # Remove axes for clean pie
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"))



⚠️ Warning: Use pie charts only for 2-5 categories!

🔴 Goal: Part of a Whole (modern alternative to pie)

# Calculate percentages for gender distribution
gender_summary <- data_clean %>%
  count(Gender) %>%
  mutate(percentage = n / sum(n) * 100)

# Create donut chart (pie with hole in center)
ggplot(gender_summary, aes(x = 2, y = n, fill = Gender)) +  # x=2 creates the hole
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1, color = "white") +
  coord_polar("y", start = 0) +
  xlim(0.5, 2.5) +  # Creates the "donut hole" effect
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +  # Use professional color palette
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(Gender, "\n", round(percentage, 1), "%")),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
            family = "serif", size = 4) +
  labs(title = "Patient Gender Distribution") +
  theme_void(base_family = "serif") +

text:
Functions covered in this module



Function
Use case




ggwithinstats()

title: ggstatsplot — Intermediate
text:
ggwithinstats() — Repeated Measures
Use this when the same participants are measured more than once (paired/within-subjects design) — for example, pre-post measurements.

library(ggstatsplot)
library(tidyr)

# Reshape from wide to long for within-subjects comparison
overall_long <- bp |>
  select(PatientID, SysBP_0m, SysBP_3m) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(SysBP_0m, SysBP_3m),
    names_to  = "timepoint",
    values_to = "sbp"
  ) |>
  mutate(timepoint = factor(timepoint,
                            levels = c("SysBP_0m", "SysBP_3m"),
                            labels = c("Baseline", "3 Months")))

ggwithinstats(
  data    = overall_long,
  x       = timepoint,
  y       = sbp,
  subject.id = PatientID,       # links pairs across timepoints
  title   = "Systolic BP: Baseline vs 3 Months"
)








Key differences from ggbetweenstats():

subject.id is required — it tells the function which rows are paired
Uses a paired t-test (parametric) or Wilcoxon signed-rank (non-parametric)
Lines connect paired observations in the plot

title: ggstatsplot — Intermediate
text:
ggbarstats() — Proportions
Use this when you want to compare proportions of a categorical outcome across groups. The output includes a χ² or Fisher’s exact test.

ggbarstats(
  data  = bp,
  x     = SmokingStatus,    # the categories whose proportions fill each bar
  y     = Region,           # the groups along the x-axis
  title = "Smoking Status by Region"
)








What the output shows:

Stacked bar chart with proportion labels
χ² test statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, and Cramér’s V effect size
Above each bar, a one-sample χ² test of whether the categories are equally common within that bar (not a comparison between bars)

Swap axes to change orientation:

# Make Region the outcome (fill) and SmokingStatus the groups
ggbarstats(data = bp, x = Region, y = SmokingStatus)

title: ggstatsplot — Intermediate
text:
ggpiestats() — Pie / Donut Charts
Use this for a single categorical variable, or two categorical variables where a pie chart is appropriate for the audience.

# Single variable — proportions in each treatment group
ggpiestats(
  data  = bp,
  x     = TreatmentGroup,
  title = "Distribution of Treatment Groups"
)









# Two variables — smoking status by treatment group
ggpiestats(
  data  = bp,
  x     = SmokingStatus,
  y     = TreatmentGroup,       # creates faceted pies
  title = "Smoking Status by Treatment Group"
)














WarningWhen to use pie charts



Pie charts are appropriate when there are ≤ 5 categories and the audience is non-technical. For more categories or detailed comparisons, prefer ggbarstats().

title: ggstatsplot — Intermediate
text:
Customising appearance
All ggstatsplot functions return a ggplot2 object, so you can extend them normally.

library(ggplot2)

ggbetweenstats(
  data        = bp,
  x           = Region,
  y           = SysBP_0m,
  # Colours for each group
  palette     = "Set2",
  package     = "RColorBrewer",
  # Remove the subtitle (statistical results) if preferred
  results.subtitle = TRUE,
  # Change point size and transparency
  point.args  = list(size = 2, alpha = 0.4),
  title       = "Systolic BP by Region"
) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  labs(caption = "Source: simulated BP dataset")








Common customisation parameters:



Parameter
What it controls




palette + package
Colour palette for groups


results.subtitle
Show/hide statistical annotation


point.args
Size, alpha, shape of data points


centrality.plotting
Show/hide mean/median marker


xlab / ylab
Axis labels

title: ggstatsplot — Intermediate
text:
Introduction to Bayes Factors
When you set type = "bayes", ggstatsplot reports a Bayes Factor (BF₁₀) instead of a p-value.

ggbetweenstats(
  data  = bp,
  x     = Region,
  y     = SysBP_0m,
  type  = "bayes",
  title = "Systolic BP by Region (Bayesian)"
)








Interpreting BF₁₀:



BF₁₀
Interpretation




> 100
Extreme evidence for H₁


30–100
Very strong evidence for H₁


10–30
Strong evidence for H₁


3–10
Moderate evidence for H₁


1–3
Anecdotal evidence for H₁


~1
No evidence either way


1/3–1
Anecdotal evidence for H₀


< 1/10
Strong–extreme evidence for H₀



ggstatsplot prints loge(BF₀₁) under the plot. Convert: BF₁₀ = 1 / BF₀₁ = exp(−loge(BF₀₁)). For the Region comparison above, loge(BF₀₁) ≈ 3.0 gives BF₀₁ ≈ 20 (BF₁₀ ≈ 0.05): strong evidence for no difference between regions, consistent with the Welch ANOVA (p = 0.65).

BF₁₀ > 3: reasonably confident that H₁ (an effect exists) is supported
BF₁₀ < 1/3: reasonably confident that H₀ (no effect) is supported
Values between 1/3 and 3 are inconclusive







Note



Bayesian inference and deeper interpretation of Bayes factors is covered in ggstatsplot — Advanced.

title: Plotting Tools
text:
This chapter introduces various tools and libraries available in R for creating visualizations. It covers base R plotting functions, as well as popular packages like ggplot2 and lattice, which offer advanced capabilities for creating complex and customizable plots.


R’s built-in plotting functions provide a solid foundation for data visualization:


# Scatter plot
plot(x = mtcars$wt, y = mtcars$mpg,
     xlab = "Weight", ylab = "Miles per Gallon",
     main = "Scatter Plot Example")

# Line plot
plot(x = 1:10, y = (1:10)^2, type = "l",
     xlab = "X", ylab = "Y^2")

# Bar plot
barplot(height = c(10, 15, 8, 12),
        names.arg = c("A", "B", "C", "D"))

# Histogram
hist(mtcars$mpg, breaks = 10,
     xlab = "Miles per Gallon",
     main = "Histogram of MPG")



# Multiple plots in one window
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))  # 2x2 grid

plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)
hist(mtcars$mpg)
boxplot(mtcars$mpg ~ mtcars$cyl)
plot(density(mtcars$mpg))

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))  # Reset to single plot




ggplot2 is the most popular R package for data visualization, based on the Grammar of Graphics:


library(ggplot2)

# Basic scatter plot
ggplot(data = mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point()

# Adding aesthetics
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(title = "MPG vs Weight by Cylinders",
       x = "Weight (1000 lbs)",
       y = "Miles per Gallon")



# Points, lines, bars
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg))

p + geom_point()           # Scatter plot
p + geom_smooth()          # Smooth line
p + geom_line()            # Line plot
p + geom_bar(stat = "identity")  # Bar plot
p + geom_histogram()       # Histogram
p + geom_boxplot()         # Box plot



# Faceting
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ cyl) +
  theme_minimal()

# Custom themes
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_bw() +
  ggtitle("Custom Theme Example")




Lattice provides trellis graphics for multivariate data:
library(lattice)

# Scatter plot matrix
splom(mtcars[, c("mpg", "wt", "hp")])

# Conditional plots
xyplot(mpg ~ wt | factor(cyl), data = mtcars,
       layout = c(3, 1))

# 3D plots
cloud(mpg ~ wt * hp, data = mtcars)





library(plotly)

# Convert ggplot to interactive
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
ggplotly(p)

# Native plotly
plot_ly(mtcars, x = ~wt, y = ~mpg, type = "scatter", mode = "markers")



library(ggvis)

# Interactive ggplot2-like syntax
mtcars %>%
  ggvis(x = ~wt, y = ~mpg) %>%
  layer_points() %>%
  add_tooltip(function(df) paste("Weight:", df$wt, "MPG:", df$mpg))






library(ggstatsplot)

# Statistical plots with tests
ggbetweenstats(data = mtcars, x = cyl, y = mpg)



library(ggplot2)
library(maps)

# Basic map
world <- map_data("world")
ggplot(world, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group)) +
  geom_polygon(fill = "lightblue", color = "black")



library(igraph)
library(ggraph)

# Create network
g <- make_ring(10)
ggraph(g, layout = "circle") +
  geom_edge_link() +
  geom_node_point(size = 5)

ggplot2: Publication-quality static plots, complex customizations

R’s built-in plotting functions provide a solid foundation for data visualization:

plot(x = mtcars$wt, y = mtcars$mpg,

section: Choosing the Right Visualization for Your Data
text:
Choosing the Right Visualization for Your Data
A Practical Framework Based on Analytical Goals

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
Your Roadmap for Visualization Selection

Identify Your Data Type

What kind of data do you have? (Numeric, Categorical, Temporal, etc.)

Define Your Analytical Goal

What do you want to communicate? (Compare, Distribute, Show Relationships, etc.)

Select the Appropriate Chart

What visualization best achieves your goal?

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
Color-Coded Framework









Goal
Symbol
Question
Purpose




Distribution
●
“What’s the spread?”
Show data spread, shape, outliers


Correlation
●
“How do things relate?”
Show relationships between variables


Ranking
●
“What’s the order?”
Compare values in order


Part of Whole
●
“What’s the composition?”
Show proportions/percentages


Evolution
●
“How does it change over time?”
Track trends and changes


Maps
●
“Where is it located?”
Geographic/spatial distribution


Flow
●
“How does it move?”
Movement, transitions, journeys

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
section: Quick Reference - What Each Color Means
text:
Quick Reference - What Each Color Means

● Gold/Yellow = Distribution - Shows data spread, frequency, shape, outliers
● Blue = Correlation - Shows relationships, associations between variables
● Green = Ranking - Shows order, comparison of values, top/bottom
● Red/Salmon = Part of Whole - Shows composition, proportions, percentages
● Light Blue = Evolution - Shows trends, changes over time, trajectories
● Purple = Maps - Shows geographic/spatial distribution, location-based data
● Pink/Tan = Flow - Shows movement, transitions, journeys, hierarchies

Tip: When you see a colored dot next to a chart name, it tells you what analytical goal that chart serves best!

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
The 6 Data Type Categories








Data Type
Definition
Examples




Numeric
Continuous measurements
Age, weight, blood pressure, lab values


Categoric
Discrete categories/groups
Gender, disease status, treatment type


Ordinal
Ordered categories
Likert scale, tumor stages, severity levels


Time Series
Temporal/chronological data
Monthly incidence, patient vitals over time


Relational
Connections/networks
Patient pathways, disease networks


Map
Geographic/spatial data
Regional disease rates, location coordinates

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
How Variables Combine
SINGLE VARIABLE
├── Numeric → Histogram, Density, Boxplot
├── Categoric → Bar, Pie, Lollipop
├── Ordinal → Ordered Bar, Cumulative Frequency
├── Time Series → Line, Area
├── Map → Choropleth, Bubble Map
└── Relational → Network Graph

BIVARIATE (TWO VARIABLES)
├── Numeric × Numeric → Scatter, Hexbin, Bubble
├── Numeric × Categoric → Boxplot, Violin, Grouped Bar
├── Categoric × Categoric → Grouped/Stacked Bar, Mosaic, Heatmap
├── Time Series × Numeric → Multi-line, Stacked Area
├── Time Series × Categoric → Faceted Line, Interaction Plot
└── Any + Relational → Sankey, Chord

MULTIVARIATE (3+ VARIABLES)
├── Numeric × Numeric × Numeric → Bubble, Faceted Scatter
├── Numeric × Multiple Categoric → Faceted Box/Violin, Interaction
├── Multiple Categoric × Multiple Categoric → Sankey, Sunburst, Treemap
├── Time Series × Multiple Variables → Ridgeline, Faceted Line
└── Hierarchical → Treemap, Sunburst, Hierarchical Edge Bundling

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution | ● Ranking | ● Part of Whole
Chart Options:

Bar Chart ● (counts/frequencies)
Lollipop Chart ● (alternative to bar, especially for long lists)
Cleveland Dot Plot ● (ranked comparison)
Pie Chart ● (≤5 categories only, part-to-whole)
Doughnut Chart ● (like pie, better labels)
Circular Bar Plot ● (aesthetic alternative)

Healthcare Examples:

Disease prevalence by state
Hospitalization by insurance type
Comorbidity frequency distribution

Decision Guide:

Few categories (<5) and need part-of-whole → Pie/Doughnut
Few-moderate categories → Bar chart (horizontal if long names)
Many categories (>8) → Lollipop or Cleveland dot
Need ranking emphasis → Ordered bar or lollipop

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution | ● Part of Whole (Ordered)
Chart Options:

Ordered Bar Chart ● (maintain categorical order)
Ordered Dot Plot ●
Cumulative Frequency Plot ● (especially for Likert scales)
Frequency Polygon ● (smooth trend)

Healthcare Examples:

Patient satisfaction (Likert: 1=Very Unsatisfied to 5=Very Satisfied)
Tumor stages frequency (Stage I → II → III → IV)
Pain severity distribution (None → Mild → Moderate → Severe)
Risk level counts (Low → Medium → High)

Decision Guide:

Likert scales → Stacked ordered bar or cumulative frequency
Natural progression (stages, severity) → Maintain order on axis
Show accumulation → Cumulative frequency plot
Compare between groups → Grouped ordered bar

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution
Chart Options:

Histogram ● (shows bin structure, distribution shape)
Density Plot ● (smooth, continuous estimate)
Boxplot ● (summary: median, quartiles, outliers)
Violin Plot ● (distribution + boxplot combined)
Dot/Strip Plot ● (individual points, best for small n)

Healthcare Examples:

Age distribution in cohort
Blood pressure measurements in population
Lab values (HbA1c, cholesterol, creatinine)
Hospital length of stay

Decision Guide:



Scenario
Best Choice
Why




n < 20
Dot/Strip plot
See every point


n = 20-100
Histogram + Boxplot
Balance detail & summary


n > 100
Density plot
Smooth, reduces noise


Want outliers
Boxplot
Shows extreme values clearly


Want shape details
Violin plot
Shows multimodality, skewness

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Evolution
Chart Options:

Line Chart ● (standard for continuous time data)
Area Chart ● (emphasizes magnitude/volume)
Streamgraph ● (stacked area with flowing theme)

Healthcare Examples:

Disease incidence trends over years
Hospital admission rates monthly
COVID-19 case counts by week
Patient vital signs during hospitalization

Decision Guide:

Single series, continuous time → Line chart
Show cumulative volume → Area chart
Multiple series, show total → Stacked area
Sparse time points → Line chart with markers

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Maps
Chart Options:

Choropleth Map ● (color-coded by region)
Bubble Map ● (circles sized by value)
Heat Map ● (geographic intensity)
Dot Map ● (point locations)

Healthcare Examples:

Regional disease rates (e.g., TB incidence by state in India)
Hospital bed density by district
Maternal mortality ratios by region
Vaccination coverage by area

Decision Guide:

Show rate/percentage by region → Choropleth
Show absolute counts by location → Bubble map
Show intensity/density → Heat map
Specific point locations matter → Dot map

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Correlation | ● Distribution
Chart Options:

Scatter Plot ● (relationship between two continuous variables)
Hexbin Plot ● (2D histogram for dense data)
2D Density Plot ● (contour or heatmap of overlapping points)
Bubble Plot ● (3rd variable via size or color)

Healthcare Examples:

Age vs BMI (body mass relationship)
HbA1c vs Blood Glucose (glycemic control markers)
Creatinine vs eGFR (kidney function)
Systolic vs Diastolic Blood Pressure

Decision Guide:



Scenario
Best Choice




Moderate sample, clear pattern
Scatter plot


Large n, lots of overplotting
Hexbin or 2D density


Want 3rd variable shown
Bubble (size) or color gradient


Focused region interest
Zoomed scatter with annotations

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution | ● Correlation (Comparison)
Chart Options:

Boxplot ● (median, quartiles, outliers by group)
Violin Plot ● (distribution shape by group)
Jittered Dot/Strip/Beeswarm Plot ● (individual points by group)
Bar Chart with Error Bars ● (mean/median ± SD/IQR)
Cleveland Dot Plot ● (ranked group means)

Healthcare Examples:

HbA1c levels across treatment arms
BMI by disease status (healthy vs diabetic vs obese)
Blood pressure by gender
Hospital length of stay by admission type

Decision Guide:



Sample Size
Distribution Focus
Summary Focus




n < 30
Dot/Strip + Boxplot
Not recommended


n = 30-100
Violin or Boxplot
Bar with error bars


n > 100
Violin plot
Density overlay + mean line


Outliers matter
Boxplot + jitter
Always show


Group ranking focus
Ranked dots
Lollipop chart

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Correlation (Probability)
Chart Options:

Logistic Regression Curve ● (smooth probability line)
Density Overlay ● (stacked densities by category)
Grouped Histogram/Density ● (overlapping distributions)

Healthcare Examples:

Disease presence/absence across age ranges
Treatment response (yes/no) by baseline score
Adverse event (yes/no) by medication dose
Mortality (yes/no) by APACHE score

Visualization:

X-axis: Numeric predictor (age, score, dose)
Y-axis: Probability or proportion
Two groups shown as overlapping curves or stacked

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
section: ● Distribution | ● Ranking | ● Part of Whole | ● Correlation
text:
● Distribution | ● Ranking | ● Part of Whole | ● Correlation
Chart Options:

Grouped Bar Chart ● (side-by-side comparison)
Dodged Bar Chart ● (similar to grouped)
Stacked Bar Chart ● (shows totals + composition)
Stacked Bar (Proportional) ● (percentage/100% stacked)
Mosaic Plot ● (area ∝ frequency, shows association)
Heatmap ● (color intensity for cell frequencies)

Healthcare Examples:

Gender vs Disease status (M/F vs HIV+/HIV-)
Treatment arm vs Adverse event (Drug A/B vs AE Yes/No)
Hospital site vs Patient outcome (Site 1-3 vs Recovered/Died)
Risk level by comorbidity count

Decision Guide:



Goal
Best Chart




Compare totals & subgroups
Grouped bar


Show composition per category
Stacked bar


Show percentages only
Stacked bar (proportional)


Detect association strength
Mosaic or heatmap


Many categories, dense
Heatmap with color gradient

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution (Ordered)
Chart Options:

Ordered Boxplot ● (boxplot by ordinal groups, maintaining order)
Ordered Violin Plot ● (violin by ordinal groups)
Ordered Jittered Points ● (points by group, groups ordered)

Healthcare Examples:

Medication efficacy vs dose level (Low/Medium/High)
Lab value vs disease severity (Stage I-IV)
Pain score vs treatment intensity (Mild/Moderate/Severe)
Functional status vs age group (Young/Middle/Elderly)

Key Point:

Always maintain explicit ordering on axis
Example: Severity I → II → III → IV (not random order)

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Evolution | ● Correlation (Trend)
Chart Options:

Line Chart ● (single series over time)
Multi-line Chart ● (multiple series overlay)
Area Chart ● (cumulative volume over time)
Stacked Area Chart ● (composition over time)
Connected Scatter ● (if sparse time points)

Healthcare Examples:

Disease incidence trends over years (single disease)
Patient vital signs over hospital stay (temperature, BP, HR)
Medication effectiveness over weeks (Drug A vs B)
Mortality rates over decades by region

Decision Guide:

Single series → Line chart
Few series (2-3) to compare → Multi-line chart
Many series, want to show total → Stacked area
Series showing parts of whole → Stacked area
Sparse measurements → Line with markers or connected scatter

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Evolution (By Group) | ● Correlation (Group Comparison)
Chart Options:

Grouped Line Chart ● (separate lines for each group)
Faceted Line Chart ● (separate subplots per group)
Grouped Area Chart ● (stacked or overlapping)
Interaction Plot ● (lines intersecting showing interaction)
Ribbon Chart ● (flowing bands representing groups)

Healthcare Examples:

Mortality rate trends (gender comparison: M vs F)
Hospital admission trends by institution (5-year follow-up)
Drug effectiveness over time by treatment arm
Complication rates by age group over study period

Decision Guide:

Few groups (2-3) → Multi-line chart
Many groups (5+) → Faceted line plots
Want to show total + groups → Stacked area
Interaction patterns matter → Interaction plot (lines cross)
Space constraints → Faceting better than overlapping

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution (Ordered) | ● Part of Whole (Ordered)
Chart Options:

Ordered Grouped Bar Chart ● (bars by category, groups ordered)
Ordered Stacked Bar ● (stacked, ordinal categories in order)
Faceted Ordered Bar ● (subplots maintaining order)

Healthcare Examples:

Patient satisfaction (Likert: 1-5) by hospital ward
Pain severity (None/Mild/Moderate/Severe) by treatment type
Risk level (Low/Med/High) by comorbidity count
Functional status by treatment arm

Key Point:

Maintain ordinal ordering on one axis
Example: Satisfaction scale always: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
3+ Continuous Variables | ● Correlation
Chart Options:

Bubble Plot ● (x, y, size = 3rd; color/opacity = 4th)
Faceted Scatter ● (scatter by groups, multiple subplots)
3D Scatter (NOT recommended: distorts perception)

Healthcare Examples:

Age vs BMI (size=cholesterol, color=treatment arm)
HbA1c vs glucose (size=insulin, faceted by gender)
Systolic vs diastolic BP (colored by smoking status)

Decision Guide:

3 variables → Bubble plot (x, y, size)
4 variables → Bubble + color
5+ variables → Multiple faceted plots (don’t try to cram)

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Correlation Matrix
Chart Options:

Correlation Matrix ● (numeric table of coefficients)
Correlogram ● (heatmap with color intensity = correlation strength)
Scatter Plot Matrix ● (pairwise scatter plots)

Healthcare Examples:

Lab inter-correlations: glucose, insulin, triglycerides, HDL, LDL
Vital signs correlations: BP, HR, RR, O2 saturation, temperature
Biomarker relationships in cohort study

Visualization:

Color intensity (warm = positive, cool = negative)
Cell size may represent correlation strength
Diagonal typically = 1.0 (variable with itself)

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution (Faceted) | ● Correlation (Interaction)
Chart Options:

Faceted Boxplot/Violin ● (boxplot per group, subplots for 3rd variable)
Interaction Plot ● (lines connecting means by two factors)
Faceted Scatter + regression lines ● (by groups)

Healthcare Examples:

HbA1c by treatment type, faceted by gender (4 subplots: 2 treat × 2 gender)
Lab values by disease status, colored by age group
Drug efficacy by dose level, faceted by patient comorbidity

Visualization Strategy:

Primary grouping on axis
Secondary grouping via facets or colors
Show interactions: do lines cross? Do patterns differ?

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Evolution (Advanced) | ● Distribution (Temporal)
Chart Options:

Multi-line Chart with Faceting ● (separate subplots per group)
Ridgeline Plot ● (distribution by group, stacked vertically)
Slope Chart ● (start → end values, multiple series)
Animated Time Series ● (interactive exploration)

Healthcare Examples:

Disease incidence over years, separate lines by region (5 regions)
Patient vitals during admission, faceted by treatment arm
Hospital census by time, colored by department

Decision Guide:

Multiple time series + groups → Faceted multi-line
Distribution evolution over time → Ridgeline plot
Show change from start to end → Slope chart

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Flow | ● Part of Whole (Hierarchical)
Chart Options:

Sankey Diagram ● (flow from one category to another)
Alluvial Diagram ● (similar to Sankey, broader flows)
Treemap ● (nested rectangles for hierarchy)
Sunburst Chart ● (nested circles/rings for hierarchy)

Healthcare Examples:

Sankey: Patient flow (admission → diagnostic → treatment → discharge)
Alluvial: Disease progression stages (diagnosis → worsening/improvement → outcome)
Treemap: Hospital structure (Region → Hospital → Department → Ward)
Sunburst: Disease classification (Category → Subcategory → Specific condition)

Decision Guide:

Flow/transition/journey → Sankey or Alluvial
Nested hierarchy/parts → Treemap or Sunburst

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Flow | ● Correlation (Connections)
Chart Options:

Sankey Diagram ● (directional flows between nodes)
Chord Diagram ● (bi-directional relationships, circular)
Network Graph ● (nodes + edges, force-directed layout)
Arc Diagram ● (nodes in line, arcs show connections)

Healthcare Examples:

Sankey: Patient journeys through clinic system
Chord: Disease co-occurrence patterns (patient network)
Network: Hospital referral patterns (which hospitals refer to which)
Arc: Comorbidity networks (which diseases co-occur)

Visualization:

Nodes = entities (patients, diseases, hospitals)
Edges/arcs/flows = relationships (referral, co-occurrence)

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Part of Whole | ● Flow
Chart Options:

Treemap ● (nested rectangles, size ∝ value)
Sunburst Chart ● (nested circles, size ∝ value)
Hierarchical Edge Bundling ● (connections in hierarchy)

Healthcare Examples:

Treemap: Hospital admissions by Region → State → Hospital → Department (size = admission count)
Sunburst: Disease classification by Category → Subcategory → Specific condition → ICD code
Hierarchical Edge Bundling: Referral patterns between hospitals at different levels

Decision Guide:

Static hierarchy focus → Treemap
Want circular aesthetic → Sunburst
Complex relationships in hierarchy → Hierarchical edge bundling

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Flow | ● Part of Whole
Waterfall Chart

Shows cumulative effect of sequential positive/negative values
Healthcare Example: Patient survival from enrollment → screening loss → randomization → completion

Start: 1000 enrolled
Drop: -50 screening failures
Drop: -30 withdrawn consent
End: 920 completed


Funnel Chart

Stages in a process, showing attrition at each step
Healthcare Example: Hospital admission pipeline

Emergency triage: 500
Admitted: 400 (20% filtered out)
Discharged: 350 (12.5% transferred)
Readmitted: 30 (8.6% recurrent)

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Evolution (Advanced) | ● Distribution (Temporal)
Streamgraph

Stacked area with flowing, organic theme
Example: Emergency admissions over time, stacked by department

Total volume trends visible + department composition


Calendar Heatmap

Daily/weekly patterns across entire year
Example: Hospital occupancy by day of week

Darker = higher occupancy
Pattern reveals peak days/seasons


Frequency Polygon

Line connecting histogram bins
Example: Age distribution comparison between cohorts

Multiple overlaid frequency polygons

Option
Chart Type
Visualization

Scenario: “Top 10 competitors’ market share over 5 years by region”
Step 1: Identify Data Type

Step 2: Define Analytical Goal

● Evolution (trends over time)
● Ranking (who’s leading?)
● Correlation (how do regions differ?)
● Composition (what % of total?)

Step 3: Chart Options







Option
Approach




A
Stacked area per region (faceted: 3-5 subplots) ● ●


B
Grouped multi-line (each region = different color) ●


C
Animated bar chart (top 10 race by region) ● ●

Best static option: Faceted stacked area (shows time, composition, region comparison)
Best interactive: Animated bar or dashboard

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
❌ What NOT to Do
❌ Pie charts with 10+ categories

Why? Human perception fails with small angles
Solution: Use bar chart ●, lollipop ●, or split into multiple pies

❌ 3D charts

Why? Perspective distorts data perception (3D cone/pyramid/sphere)
Solution: Stick to 2D representations

❌ Dual-axis charts

Why? Can mislead by manipulating axis scales
Solution: Use faceting or separate plots instead

❌ Wrong color coding

Why? Color should reinforce analytical goal (not random aesthetic)
Solution: Sequential colors for magnitude, categorical colors for groups

❌ Overplotting (overlapping points)

Why? Can’t see density or exact position
Solution: Use transparency (alpha), jitter, hexbin ●, or density plots ●

❌ Stacked bars for detailed comparison

Why? Only first and last categories are easy to compare
Solution: Use grouped bar ● or faceting for detailed comparison

❌ Too many dimensions on one plot

Why? Cognitive overload, hard to extract insight
Solution: Split into multiple focused visualizations

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
Core Principles for Effective Visualization
✅ Always start with your analytical goal - What question are you answering? (distribute, compare, rank, relate, etc.)
✅ Data types narrow your options significantly - Numeric vs Categoric vs Ordinal vs Temporal vs Spatial
✅ Multiple valid charts may exist—choose based on audience & context - Scientist ≠ Executive ≠ Patient communication
✅ Use color strategically to support your analytical goal - Sequential for magnitude, categorical for groups, diverging for contrasts
✅ Simplicity trumps complexity; avoid unnecessary dimensions - If 3D doesn’t add insight, keep it 2D - If faceting helps clarity, use it
✅ When in doubt, check data-to-viz.com or reference examples - Don’t reinvent the wheel; learn from established best practices
✅ Practice makes perfect—iterate on visualizations - First draft rarely optimal; refine based on feedback
