title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
What is Grammar of Graphics?

A systematic framework for creating visualizations
Developed by Leland Wilkinson, implemented in ggplot2 by Hadley Wickham
Treats plots as layered compositions of graphical elements
Separates data from aesthetics from geometry
Enables infinite combinations from finite components
More flexible than traditional plotting systems


Core Philosophy: Build complex visualizations by combining simple, well-defined layers

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
Why ggplot2?

Consistent syntax across all plot types
Flexible and extensible - easy to customize
Professional quality output
Reproducible - code-based approach
Large ecosystem of extensions
Industry standard in R community


vs Base R: More intuitive, consistent, and powerful for complex visualizations

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
The Seven Layers of Grammar

Data - The dataset being visualized
Aesthetics - Mapping data to visual properties
Geometries - Visual marks (points, lines, bars)
Statistics - Data transformations and summaries
Coordinates - The plotting space and axes
Facets - Subplots for data subsets
Scales - Mapping data values to aesthetics


Plus: Themes for overall visual styling

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
1. Data Layer
The foundation of every ggplot2 visualization

Must be a data frame or tibble
Each row represents an observation
Each column represents a variable
Data should be in tidy format

Each variable in one column
Each observation in one row
Each value in one cell




Code
# Basic structure
ggplot(data = my_data)

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
2. Aesthetics (aes)
Mapping data variables to visual properties

Position: x, y
Color: color (points/lines), fill (areas)
Size: size of points or line width
Shape: point shapes
Transparency: alpha (0 = transparent, 1 = opaque)
Line type: linetype (solid, dashed, dotted)
Group: group (for grouping data)



Code
ggplot(data, aes(x = var1, y = var2, color = var3))

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
3. Geometries (geom)
Visual representations of data

geom_point() - Scatter plots
geom_line() - Line graphs
geom_bar() / geom_col() - Bar charts
geom_histogram() - Histograms
geom_boxplot() - Box plots
geom_violin() - Violin plots
geom_smooth() - Smoothed conditional means
And many more…


Key concept: Geoms are added as layers with +

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
4. Statistics (stat)
Data transformations and summaries

Many geoms have default statistics
stat_identity - Use data as-is
stat_count - Count observations
stat_bin - Bin data into groups
stat_smooth - Add smoothed line
stat_summary - Compute summary statistics


Usually implicit: Most geoms automatically apply appropriate statistics

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
5. Coordinates (coord)
Defining the plotting space

coord_cartesian() - Default Cartesian coordinates
coord_flip() - Flip x and y axes
coord_polar() - Polar coordinates
coord_fixed() - Fixed aspect ratio
coord_trans() - Transformed coordinates



Code
# Flip axes for horizontal bars
ggplot(data, aes(x = category, y = value)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip()

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
6. Facets
Creating subplots for data subsets

facet_wrap() - Wrap panels by one variable
facet_grid() - Grid of panels by two variables
Useful for comparing groups
Can have free or fixed scales



Code
# Facet by one variable
facet_wrap(~ treatment_group)

# Facet by two variables
facet_grid(gender ~ region)

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
7. Scales
Mapping data values to aesthetic properties

Control how data maps to aesthetics
scale_x_continuous() - Continuous x-axis
scale_color_manual() - Manual color specification
scale_fill_brewer() - ColorBrewer palettes
scale_y_log10() - Logarithmic transformation
Control breaks, limits, labels, transformations



Code
scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "blue", "green"))

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
8. Guides (Legends & Axes)
Helping readers interpret the plot

Axes: Show scale of position aesthetics
Legends: Show scale of other aesthetics (color, size, shape)
Controlled by guides() function
Can be positioned, styled, or removed
Automatically generated from aesthetics



Code
guides(color = guide_legend(title = "Treatment Group"))

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
Building Plots Progressively
The power of layering

ggplot(data, aes(x = age, y = systolic_bp)) +        # 1. Data + aesthetics
  geom_point() +                                       # 2. Add points
  geom_smooth() +                                      # 3. Add trend line
  facet_wrap(~ treatment_group) +                      # 4. Add facets
  theme_minimal()                                      # 5. Apply theme


Each layer builds on the previous, creating complex visualizations from simple components

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
Data Preparation

# Create derived variables
bp_data <- bp_data %>%
  mutate(
    # BP change from baseline to 6 months
    SysBP_Change = SysBP_6m - SysBP_0m,
    DiaBP_Change = DiaBP_6m - DiaBP_0m,
    
    # Age groups
    AgeGroup = cut(Age, 
                   breaks = c(0, 30, 50, 65, 100),
                   labels = c("18-30", "31-50", "51-65", "65+")),
    
    # Hypertension status (Systolic ≥140 or Diastolic ≥90)
    Hypertension_Baseline = ifelse(SysBP_0m >= 140 | DiaBP_0m >= 90, 
                                   "Hypertensive", "Normal"),
    
    # BMI categories
    BMI_Category = cut(BMI,
                       breaks = c(0, 18.5, 25, 30, 100),
                       labels = c("Underweight", "Normal", "Overweight", "Obese"))
  )

Handling Missing Data

# Check missing data
missing_summary <- bp_data %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~sum(is.na(.))))

# Display columns with missing data

  select(where(~. > 0))

1            2              2

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
Handling Missing Data: Strategies

# Strategy 1: Filter complete cases for specific analysis
bp_complete <- bp_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(ExerciseFreq), !is.na(ChronicDisease))

# Strategy 2: Use na.rm in calculations
bp_data %>%
  group_by(TreatmentGroup) %>%
  summarise(Mean_SysBP = mean(SysBP_0m, na.rm = TRUE))

# Strategy 3: Explicitly show missing as category
bp_data %>%
  mutate(ExerciseFreq = replace_na(ExerciseFreq, "Unknown"))

title: Data Viz Caveats: Flash Cards
text:
A checklist of the mistakes that most often make a chart mislead or confuse, as 70 flash cards in 8 groups. Read the title, decide what the problem is and how you would fix it, then open the card. Use Practise to be dealt the cards one at a time; the ones you mark Review again come back first.
Most of these points are taught in Best Practices, Matching Data to Plots and the ggplot2 modules; each card links to where. The list of topics follows the caveats collection of data-to-viz.com by Yan Holtz and Conor Healy, where many cards have a longer illustrated page (the “data-to-viz” link on the card). The wording and the R code here are our own.

title: Data Viz Caveats: Flash Cards
text:
Misleading charts




Do not cut the y-axis of a bar chart

Problem. Bars encode values by their length. Starting the axis at 120 mmHg makes a 3 mmHg gap look like a doubling.
Fix. Start bar charts at zero. If the differences matter but are small, show points with confidence intervals instead of bars.
ggplot(d, aes(group, sbp)) + geom_col() + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA))
In the course: Best Practices · data-to-viz





Box plots hide the shape

Problem. Two groups can have identical boxes while one is bimodal and the other is not; small groups look as solid as large ones.
Fix. Add the raw points (jittered), or use a violin or raincloud, and print the n per group.
geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) + geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.4)
In the course: Merged Visuals · data-to-viz





Avoid counter-intuitive encodings

Problem. Readers expect up = more, red = bad, bigger = larger. An inverted axis or a reversed colour scale makes them read the opposite of the truth.
Fix. Keep the usual direction; if you must invert (e.g. ranks), say so on the axis and in the title.
data-to-viz





Bars with error bars (“dynamite plots”) hide the data

Problem. A bar of the mean with an error bar shows two numbers and suggests values below the mean are the only ones that exist.
Fix. Show the individual points with the mean and its 95% CI, or a box/violin plot. State whether bars are SD, SE or CI.
stat_summary(fun.data = mean_cl_normal, geom = 'pointrange') + geom_jitter(alpha = 0.3)
In the course: Statistical Plots · data-to-viz





Be wary of two y-axes

Problem. The scales of the two axes are arbitrary, so any two series can be made to cross, diverge or move together.
Fix. Use two panels with a shared x-axis, or index both series to 100 at the start.
facet_wrap(~ series, ncol = 1, scales = 'free_y')
In the course: Matching Data to Plots · data-to-viz





Avoid 3D

Problem. Perspective makes nearer bars and slices look bigger and hides some values behind others.
Fix. Use the 2D version. Three numeric variables? Colour or size for the third, or small multiples.
In the course: Matching Data to Plots · data-to-viz





Do not cherry-pick the data

Problem. Choosing the start date, the sites or the subgroup that tells the best story misleads even when every point is correct.
Fix. Show the full period and all groups, and say why any are left out.





Draw proportions accurately

Problem. Icons or shapes scaled by height and width (both) exaggerate differences; a doubled value looks four times larger.
Fix. Make area (not radius or height and width together) proportional to the value, or simply use bars.





Respect time intervals

Problem. Unevenly spaced dates (2010, 2015, 2020, 2021, 2022) drawn at equal distances distort the trend.
Fix. Use a real date or numeric x-axis so the gaps are drawn to scale.
aes(x = as.Date(visit_date))   # not factor(visit_date)





Show the sample size

Problem. A percentage from 8 people looks as solid as one from 800.
Fix. Print the n on the axis labels, in the legend or in a caption; add confidence intervals.
scale_x_discrete(labels = \(x) paste0(x, '\n(n = ', table(d$group)[x], ')'))





Beware of Simpson’s paradox

Problem. A trend in the pooled data can reverse inside every subgroup when the groups differ in size and level.
Fix. Colour or facet by the likely confounder before drawing a conclusion; adjust for it in the model.
ggplot(d, aes(x, y, colour = group)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = 'lm')
In the course: Regression Analysis · data-to-viz

title: Data Viz Caveats: Flash Cards
text:
Wrong chart type




Many thin lollipops or bars can shimmer

Problem. Dozens of closely spaced thin lines create a moiré pattern that is tiring to look at.
Fix. Use fewer, thicker bars, or a dot plot, or aggregate into groups.





The trouble with pie charts

Problem. People compare angles and areas poorly; slices of 23% and 27% look the same, and more than 5 slices are unreadable.
Fix. A sorted bar chart. Keep a pie only for 2–3 parts of a whole for a general audience.
ggplot(d, aes(reorder(cause, n), n)) + geom_col() + coord_flip()
In the course: Best Practices · data-to-viz





Radial bars distort length

Problem. In a circular bar chart the outer bars are longer than inner bars of the same value.
Fix. Use straight bars; keep radial layouts for a decorative overview with labels on the values.
data-to-viz





Maybe you do not need a map

Problem. A map draws attention to large, empty areas; if geography is not the question, it wastes space.
Fix. A sorted bar or dot chart of the regions answers “which is highest?” better than a map.
In the course: Maps and Choropleths





Two values per group? Try a dumbbell

Problem. Grouped bars for before/after (or men/women) make the reader compare bars across pairs.
Fix. A dumbbell (two points joined by a line) shows both values and the change in one glance.
geom_segment(aes(x = before, xend = after, y = site, yend = site)) + geom_point(aes(before, site)) + geom_point(aes(after, site))
In the course: Showcase





Use circular bar plots with care

Problem. Without a radial axis readers cannot read values, and the shape is driven by the order of the bars.
Fix. Label each bar with its value and sort it; prefer a straight bar chart for comparison.
data-to-viz

title: Data Viz Caveats: Flash Cards
text:
Colour




Use colour on purpose

Problem. Colouring every bar differently adds a legend and implies groups that mean nothing.
Fix. One colour by default; add colour only to encode a variable or to highlight the message (grey + one accent).
geom_col(aes(fill = site == 'Hospital B')) + scale_fill_manual(values = c('grey70', '#C0392B'), guide = 'none')
In the course: Best Practices · data-to-viz





Choose the background on purpose

Problem. A dark or coloured panel background reduces contrast and changes how colours look.
Fix. White or very light grey backgrounds; theme_minimal() or theme_classic().





Keep enough contrast

Problem. Light-yellow lines or pale text on white disappear on a projector and in print.
Fix. Check contrast (text should be dark); avoid the lightest end of a palette for thin lines and text.





Avoid pure, saturated colours

Problem. Pure red, green and blue (#FF0000 …) vibrate next to each other and tire the eye.
Fix. Muted palettes (viridis, ColorBrewer, Okabe-Ito) with one stronger colour for emphasis.





Numbers need a sequential palette

Problem. A rainbow or qualitative palette on a numeric variable has no visual order.
Fix. One hue from light to dark (or viridis) so darker = more.
scale_fill_viridis_c()   # or scale_fill_distiller(palette = 'Blues', direction = 1)
In the course: ggplot2 Module 3





Too many colours kill the story

Problem. Beyond about 6 colours readers cannot match lines to the legend.
Fix. Highlight 1–3 groups and grey the rest, or use small multiples.
In the course: Best Practices





No gradient for unordered groups

Problem. A light-to-dark gradient on regions or treatments suggests an order that does not exist.
Fix. A qualitative palette (scale_colour_brewer(palette = ‘Set2’) or Okabe-Ito) for categories.





Avoid the rainbow palette

Problem. Rainbow scales have sudden bright bands (yellow, cyan) that create boundaries not in the data, and fail in greyscale.
Fix. viridis or a single-hue sequential scale.
data-to-viz





Diverging data, diverging palette

Problem. Change from baseline, residuals and correlations have a meaningful zero that a sequential palette hides.
Fix. Two hues meeting at a neutral colour placed exactly at the midpoint.
scale_fill_gradient2(low = '#2166AC', mid = 'white', high = '#B2182B', midpoint = 0)
In the course: ggplot2 Module 3





Think of colour-blind readers

Problem. About 1 in 12 men cannot tell red from green.
Fix. Colour-blind-safe palettes (viridis, Okabe-Ito), plus redundant cues (shape, direct labels).
scale_colour_viridis_d()
In the course: Best Practices

title: Data Viz Caveats: Flash Cards
text:
Design




Align everything with something

Problem. Titles, panels and annotations that float at random positions look messy and hard to scan.
Fix. Left-align title, subtitle and caption with the plot; use the same margins across panels.
theme(plot.title.position = 'plot', plot.caption.position = 'plot')





Two fonts are enough

Problem. Many fonts and styles compete for attention.
Fix. One font family; vary size and weight for hierarchy.





Do you need that box?

Problem. Borders around the panel, legend and plot add ink without information.
Fix. Remove panel borders and legend boxes; let white space separate elements.
theme(panel.border = element_blank(), legend.background = element_blank())





Font size matters

Problem. Default 11 pt axis text is unreadable on a slide or a printed half-page.
Fix. Set base_size for the output (about 14–18 for slides); check the figure at its final size.
theme_minimal(base_size = 16)





Group what belongs together

Problem. Related bars or panels far apart force the eye to jump.
Fix. Order categories so comparisons are adjacent; group panels by the question they answer.





Make the title say something

Problem. A title like “SBP by group” makes the reader find the message themselves.
Fix. State the finding in the title (“SBP fell by 9 mmHg with the intervention”) and keep the description in the subtitle.
In the course: Best Practices





Declutter

Problem. Heavy grids, tick marks, borders and legends compete with the data.
Fix. Light or no grid lines, direct labels instead of legends, no redundant text.
In the course: Best Practices · data-to-viz

title: Data Viz Caveats: Flash Cards
text:
Maps




Do not move regions around

Problem. Moving or resizing islands and remote areas to fit the frame changes their apparent size and position.
Fix. If you must inset a region, frame it and say so; keep the same projection.





Mind the projection

Problem. Web Mercator inflates areas far from the equator, so a choropleth over-weights them.
Fix. Use an equal-area or local projected CRS for thematic maps (e.g. UTM for a district).
st_transform(blocks, 32644)
In the course: Spatial Data with sf





Normalise your maps

Problem. A map of counts is mostly a map of where people live.
Fix. Map rates (per 100,000) or ratios to expected; show counts only when workload is the question.
mutate(rate = cases / population * 1e5)
In the course: Maps and Choropleths · data-to-viz





Show missing data as missing

Problem. A missing area coloured like the lowest class looks like “no disease”.
Fix. Give missing areas a distinct neutral colour or hatching and a legend entry.
scale_fill_viridis_c(na.value = 'grey85')





Do not let small regions vanish

Problem. Dense urban wards are tiny on a map, though they hold most people.
Fix. Add an inset or zoom, a cartogram, or a hexagon tile map.
In the course: Geographic Advanced

title: Data Viz Caveats: Flash Cards
text:
Labels and legends




Prefer horizontal labels

Problem. Rotated axis labels are hard to read.
Fix. Flip the axes so long category names sit horizontally.
ggplot(d, aes(n, reorder(diagnosis, n))) + geom_col()
In the course: Best Practices · data-to-viz





Use legends sparingly

Problem. A legend makes the eye jump back and forth.
Fix. Label lines and groups directly at their ends; drop the legend.
geom_text(data = last_points, aes(label = group), hjust = 0) + theme(legend.position = 'none')





Do not put labels on top of the data

Problem. Text over points or lines hides what it describes.
Fix. Offset labels, use ggrepel, or place them in empty space.
ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = name))





Round your numbers

Problem. A value like “37.4285%” suggests a precision the data do not have and is harder to read.
Fix. Round to what matters (37%); use scales::percent() for axes.
scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent)





Annotation is crucial

Problem. Readers miss the event or threshold that explains the pattern.
Fix. Add a short note, a reference line or a shaded period where it matters.
geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date('2024-06-01'), linetype = 2) + annotate('text', ...)
data-to-viz





Do not label every tick

Problem. A label on every year or category crowds the axis.
Fix. Fewer, round breaks.
scale_x_date(date_breaks = '6 months', date_labels = '%b %Y')

title: Data Viz Caveats: Flash Cards
text:
Dashboards and data stories




Keep colours consistent across charts

Problem. If “Intervention” is blue in one panel and orange in the next, readers mis-match them.
Fix. A named colour vector used by every plot.
arm_cols <- c(Control = 'grey50', Intervention = '#2C5F8D'); scale_colour_manual(values = arm_cols)
data-to-viz





Share the y-axis to compare panels

Problem. Panels with their own y range look similar even when one is ten times higher.
Fix. Keep scales fixed when the panels are compared (the facet default); free them only to show shape.





Leave margins between charts

Problem. Panels pressed together read as one figure.
Fix. Space and alignment between panels (patchwork handles both).





Link charts that share an axis

Problem. Separate charts with the same x (time) are hard to read together.
Fix. Stack them vertically with aligned x-axes, or link them interactively (crosstalk).
In the course: Interactive Plots

title: Data Viz Caveats: Flash Cards
text:
Other




Sort your bar chart

Problem. Alphabetical order hides the ranking.
Fix. Order bars by value (unless the categories have their own order, like age groups).
aes(x = reorder(region, rate))   # or forcats::fct_reorder()
In the course: Basic Plot Gallery · data-to-viz





Histograms - mind the bin width

Problem. The same data can look smooth, bimodal or noisy depending on the bins.
Fix. Try several widths and choose a meaningful one (5 mmHg, 1 year); report it.
geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, boundary = 0)
data-to-viz





Size bubbles by area, not radius

Problem. If the radius doubles, the area quadruples.
Fix. ggplot2’s scale_size() already maps to area; avoid scale_radius().
scale_size_area(max_size = 12)
data-to-viz





The spaghetti plot

Problem. Twenty overlapping lines are unreadable.
Fix. Grey all lines and highlight one or a few, or small multiples with the others in grey behind.
In the course: Showcase · data-to-viz





Connect only connected dots

Problem. A line implies continuity between points; joining unrelated categories invents a trend.
Fix. Lines for ordered x (time, dose); points or bars for categories.
In the course: ggplot2 Module 1 · data-to-viz





Drawing order matters

Problem. The layer drawn last hides the others: a large group can bury a small one.
Fix. Draw the highlight last; use transparency.
geom_point(data = others, colour = 'grey') + geom_point(data = highlight, colour = 'red')
In the course: ggplot2 Module 4





Overlapping sets? Use an UpSet plot

Problem. Venn diagrams with more than three sets (e.g. comorbidities) are unreadable.
Fix. An UpSet plot shows the size of every intersection as a bar.





Stacked charts are hard to read

Problem. Only the bottom segment has a common baseline; the rest cannot be compared.
Fix. Grouped bars, small multiples, or 100% stacks with few segments.
In the course: Matching Data to Plots · data-to-viz





Mind the aspect ratio

Problem. Stretching a plot changes how steep a trend looks.
Fix. Choose the width/height on purpose (about 45° for the main slopes); set it in ggsave().
ggsave('fig.png', width = 7, height = 4)
data-to-viz





Make date axes easy to read

Problem. Default date labels can be dense or ambiguous (01/02).
Fix. Unambiguous formats (“Jan 2025”) and sensible breaks.
scale_x_date(date_labels = '%b %Y')





Reorder your heat map

Problem. Rows and columns in input order hide any structure.
Fix. Order by a summary or by clustering so similar rows sit together.
aes(y = fct_reorder(ward, cases, .fun = sum))
In the course: Showcase · data-to-viz





Beware of overplotting

Problem. With thousands of points the scatter becomes a solid blob.
Fix. Transparency, smaller points, hexbins or 2D density.
geom_point(alpha = 0.2)   # or geom_hex()
In the course: Intermediate Plot Gallery · data-to-viz





Too many distributions at once

Problem. Overlaid densities or histograms for many groups become a tangle.
Fix. A ridgeline plot, small multiples or box plots side by side.
ggridges::geom_density_ridges()
data-to-viz





Small multiples - rows or columns?

Problem. The layout decides what is easy to compare: aligned y values compare across a row, aligned x values down a column.
Fix. Put panels in one row to compare heights, in one column to compare positions on x.
facet_wrap(~ group, nrow = 1)
data-to-viz





Check the numbers on the chart

Problem. Percentages that do not add to 100, or totals that do not match the table, destroy trust.
Fix. Compute labels from the data in code; never type them by hand.
data-to-viz





Do not make readers do arithmetic

Problem. If the message is a difference, two lines make the reader subtract in their head.
Fix. Plot the difference itself (with its CI).
data-to-viz





Area is a weak encoding

Problem. People underestimate area differences; bubbles and treemaps give rough impressions only.
Fix. Use position or length when exact comparison matters.
data-to-viz





Grouped bars must look grouped

Problem. Evenly spaced bars hide which belong together.
Fix. Dodge within a group and leave a gap between groups.
geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.7)
data-to-viz





Radar (spider) charts mislead

Problem. The area depends on the order of the axes, and values are hard to read.
Fix. A dot plot or parallel coordinates for several measures per item.
data-to-viz





Log scales for rates of change

Problem. On a linear axis exponential growth looks explosive and early changes look flat.
Fix. A log axis when relative change is the question; label it clearly.
scale_y_log10(labels = scales::comma)





It is “choropleth”

Problem. The common misspelling “chloropleth” undermines a report.
Fix. choro (area) + pleth (quantity).

title: Data Viz Caveats: Flash Cards
text:
Self-check quiz

A chart shows the mean SBP of two arms as bars with error bars, the y-axis starting at 120 mmHg. How many caveats does it break?

None: the error bars make it an honest chart
One: the error bars alone are wrong
Two: the cut axis and the bar of means
One: just the axis start is wrong



You map dengue cases (counts) per block. What should you map instead, and why?

Cases per 100,000, so population does not drive it
The log of the counts, to compress the colour scale
Cases per km², so that large blocks look smaller
The rank of each count, so classes have equal size



Twenty ward lines overlap on one time-series chart. Which fix keeps every ward visible?

Give each of the wards its own bright, saturated colour
Small multiples, each ward over the rest in grey
A 3D chart with one ward per depth level
A dual y-axis for the larger and smaller wards



Change in SBP from baseline (negative and positive) is shown on a map. Which palette fits?

A rainbow palette from red to violet
A single-hue palette from light to dark blue
A qualitative palette with one hue per block
A diverging palette with white at zero


Your score:  (first attempt counts)

quarto render report.qmd -P region:South


Citable figure / table
#| label: fig-bp / tbl-base, then @fig-bp


PDF output
needs LaTeX: tinytex::install_tinytex()


Save a ggplot
ggsave("f.png", p, width = 7, height = 5, dpi = 300); .pdf / .svg for vector


Base graphics
png("f.png"); plot(x); dev.off()



300 dpi for print, 72–150 for screen. Interactive: plotly::ggplotly(p).

title: Best Practices
text:
Introduction to Data Visualization

“The simple graph has brought more information to the data analyst’s mind than any other device.” - John Tukey


Data visualization transforms complex data into visual insights
Good visualizations tell a story
Poor visualizations mislead or confuse
Every choice matters - especially in healthcare

title: Best Practices
text:
The Big Idea
Can you summarize your message in one sentence?

Your “Big Idea” should be:

Articulate your point of view: What do you want your audience to know?
Convey what’s at stake: Why does this matter?
Be a complete sentence: Not just a topic, but a statement

Example: “We should implement early discharge planning because it reduces readmissions by 35%”

title: Best Practices
section: Principle 1: Choose the Right Chart Type
text:
Principle 1: Choose the Right Chart Type
Match your visualization to your data and message
Different types of data require different visualizations:

Simple text: 1-2 key numbers
Tables: Multiple precise values
Categorical: Bar charts (horizontal preferred)
Continuous over time: Line charts, area charts
Distributions: Histograms, boxplots, violin plots, density plots
Relationships: Scatter plots, correlations
Comparisons: Slopegraphs, small multiples
Part-to-whole: Stacked bars (avoid pie charts)

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Simple Text


Effective: When you have just 1-2 key numbers, text is more impactful than a chart. Makes the metric impossible to miss and allows for immediate comprehension.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Table


Effective: Tables excel when precise values matter and units differ. Better than charts when readers need exact numbers for comparison or reference.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Heatmap


Effective: Heatmaps encode values with color, making patterns instantly visible in large tables. Ideal for spotting trends across two categorical dimensions.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Horizontal Bar Chart


Effective: Horizontal bars are preferred for categorical comparisons. Long labels read naturally, and length comparisons are easier than height comparisons.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Grouped Bar Chart


Effective: Grouped bars allow direct comparison across two categorical variables. The gap between groups creates visual separation that aids comprehension.

title: Best Practices
section: Avoid: Vertical Bars with Long Labels
text:
Avoid: Vertical Bars with Long Labels


Ineffective: Vertical bars with long labels force text rotation, making reading difficult. Horizontal bars solve this problem naturally.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Line Chart


Effective: Line charts emphasize continuity and trend direction over time. The connecting line helps viewers see patterns and predict future values.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Area Chart


Effective: Stacked area charts show both individual trends and cumulative total. The filled areas emphasize volume and make the overall trend prominent.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Multiple Line Series


Effective: Multiple series work when normalized to comparable scales. Different colors distinguish series while the shared timeline enables pattern comparison across variables.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Scatter Plot


Effective: Scatter plots reveal relationships between continuous variables. The trend line and confidence interval quantify the strength and uncertainty of the relationship.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Scatter with Categories


Effective: Adding categories to scatter plots reveals whether relationships hold across subgroups. Parallel slopes suggest consistent effects; diverging slopes indicate interactions.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Boxplot


Effective: Boxplots show distribution shape through quartiles. The box contains 50% of data, whiskers show range, and outliers appear as points - all in one compact visual.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Violin Plot


Effective: Violin plots reveal distribution details that boxplots hide. The width at each point shows density, making bimodal distributions and skewness immediately apparent.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Density Plot


Effective: Density plots show smooth distribution curves, ideal for comparing shapes between groups. Overlapping areas make differences in location, spread, and skewness clear.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Ridgeline Plot


Effective: Ridgeline plots stack density curves for easy comparison across many categories. The slight overlap creates visual flow while maintaining distinct distributions.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Slopegraph


Effective: Slopegraphs excel at showing change between two time points. The slope angle immediately conveys magnitude and direction of change for each entity.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Stacked Bar Chart


Effective: Stacked bars show part-to-whole relationships over time. Total height shows cumulative volume while segment heights reveal individual contributions.

title: Best Practices
section: Avoid: Y-Axis Not Starting at Zero
text:
Avoid: Y-Axis Not Starting at Zero


Ineffective: Truncating the Y-axis on bar charts distorts proportional relationships. What is actually a 3% difference appears as a 3-fold difference due to the missing baseline.

title: Best Practices
text:
Better: Y-Axis Starting at Zero


Effective: Starting bar charts at zero shows true proportions. Now it’s clear that all hospitals perform similarly at high levels with minimal variation.

title: Best Practices
text:
Avoid: Pie Charts


Ineffective: Humans struggle with angle and area estimation. Quick: is Respiratory or Other larger? Pie charts make simple comparisons unnecessarily difficult.

title: Best Practices
text:
Better: Horizontal Bar Chart


Effective: Horizontal bars make comparisons effortless. Rankings are immediately clear, and length differences are precisely perceivable unlike angles in pie charts.

title: Best Practices
text:
Principle 2: Eliminate Clutter
Remove anything that doesn’t add value

Remove chart borders and backgrounds
Lighten or remove gridlines

Remove redundant data labels
Direct labeling > legends (Gestalt principle of connection)
Clean up axis labels
Maximize data-to-ink ratio (Tufte’s principle)

title: Best Practices
text:
Data-to-Ink Ratio: Maximizing Information
Every drop of ink should represent data

Data ink: Ink that represents actual data points
Non-data ink: Gridlines, borders, backgrounds, decorations
Goal: Maximize the ratio of data ink to total ink
Remove chart junk: 3D effects, unnecessary colors, decorative elements
Keep only what serves comprehension

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: Default Plot (Cluttered)


Ineffective: Gray background, heavy gridlines, legend requiring eye travel, and borders all compete for attention. The data-to-ink ratio is low - most ink conveys no data.

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: Decluttered with Direct Labels


Effective: High data-to-ink ratio achieved by removing backgrounds, excess gridlines, and legend. Direct labels connect to data via proximity (Gestalt principle).

title: Best Practices
text:
Principle 3: Use Preattentive Attributes
Attention with attributes processed in <250ms

Color: Most powerful
Size: Indicates importance
Position: Spatial relationships
Intensity: Bold vs light
Use strategically - don’t dilute attention

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: All Equal (No Focus)


Ineffective: All bars are equal - where should the viewer look? No visual hierarchy means no clear message.

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: Strategic Highlighting


Effective: Red instantly draws the eye to the problem. Gray provides context without competing for attention.

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: Using Size for Emphasis


Effective: Size combined with color creates a clear hierarchy. The large red point in August demands attention while smaller gray points provide context.

title: Best Practices
text:
Principle 4: Gray and Bold Technique
Use color to highlight, gray to push back

Bold color for what matters most
Gray for supporting context
Maximum one bold color per chart
Creates instant visual hierarchy
Reduces cognitive load

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: Too Many Colors


Ineffective: Multiple bold colors fragment attention. When everything demands attention, nothing gets it.

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: Gray and Bold Applied


Effective: One bold color directs attention immediately to the problem area. Gray bars provide necessary context without distraction.

title: Best Practices
text:
Principle 5: Think Like a Designer
Visual design principles enhance communication

Accessibility: Colorblind-safe palettes
Alignment: Create invisible structure
White space: Let your data breathe
Contrast: Guide the eye
Typography: Readable, professional fonts

title: Best Practices
text:
Accessibility: Colorblind-Safe Palettes


Always use colorblind-safe palettes. Approximately 8% of men and 0.5% of women have color vision deficiency. Blue-orange combinations work for nearly everyone.

title: Best Practices
text:
Design Principles: Alignment & Spacing


Effective design: Generous margins, aligned text, strategic white space, and clear visual hierarchy make the message instantly clear and professional.

title: Best Practices
text:
Using Annotations Strategically


Annotations tell the story. The chart clearly shows what happened, when it happened, and why it matters - the viewer doesn’t need to guess.

title: Best Practices
text:
Before/After: Design Transformation


Design transformation: horizontal orientation, strategic color, descriptive title, reference line, and clean styling create a professional, focused message.

title: Best Practices
section: Principle 6: Tell a Story with Data
text:
Principle 6: Tell a Story with Data
Transform insights into narrative

Beginning: Set context (current state)
Middle: Show the problem/opportunity
End: Recommend action
Use descriptive titles that state your point
Guide your audience through the data

title: Best Practices
text:
Narrative vs Descriptive Titles


Narrative titles tell the story. The right chart doesn’t just show data - it communicates the achievement and its magnitude immediately.

title: Best Practices
text:
Small Multiples: Powerful Comparisons


Small multiples enable comparison. Same scales across panels make differences immediately visible. Trend lines show improvement rates at a glance.

title: Best Practices
text:
Small Multiples: Distribution Comparisons


Distribution comparison made easy. Procedure C clearly clusters below the target with minimal variation, while Procedure D shows high variability and longer recovery.

title: Best Practices
text:
Complete Story Example


Complete narrative: Beginning (context with peers), middle (intervention and dramatic improvement), end (current state showing success). Every element supports the story.

title: Best Practices
text:
Advanced Topic: Handling Uncertainty


Show uncertainty honestly. Confidence intervals demonstrate that even accounting for variability, the new treatment shows meaningful improvement over the standard.

title: Best Practices
text:
Advanced Topic: Distribution of Uncertainty


Full distribution view. The minimal overlap between distributions shows that the new treatment improvement is robust, not just a result of a few outliers.

title: Best Practices
text:
Advanced Topic: Correlation Matrices


Multivariate relationships at a glance. Correlation matrices reveal complex patterns - here showing BMI and stress as strongest blood pressure predictors.

title: Best Practices
text:
Common Pitfall: Cherry-Picking Time Ranges


Always show full context. The “growth” story disappears when viewing the complete timeline. Cherry-picking ranges is a common way to mislead.

title: Best Practices
section: Edge Case: When Breaking Rules Makes Sense
text:
Edge Case: When Breaking Rules Makes Sense


Breaking the “zero baseline” rule is appropriate when zero is meaningless (temperature, stock prices, pH). The focus should be on clinically meaningful variation.

title: Best Practices
text:
Summary: Six Core Principles

Choose the Right Chart Type - Match visualization to data and message
Eliminate Clutter - Maximize data-to-ink ratio
Use Preattentive Attributes - Guide attention strategically
Apply Gray and Bold - Create visual hierarchy
Think Like a Designer - Professional, accessible presentation
Tell a Story - Transform insights into narrative

title: Best Practices
text:
Key Takeaways

Every choice matters - color, position, size, titles
Less is more - remove everything that doesn’t serve the message
Context is crucial - never cherry-pick data ranges
Accessibility counts - use colorblind-safe palettes
Focus attention - one bold color, clear hierarchy
Tell the story - guide your audience to action

title: Best Practices
text:
When to Break the Rules
Rules are guidelines, not laws

Zero baseline: not for temperature, stock prices, or indices
Pie charts: acceptable for simple two-part comparisons
Multiple colors: when showing categorical data without hierarchy
The test: Does breaking the rule serve your audience better?
Always ask: Am I making the data clearer or just different?

title: Best Practices
text:
Resources & Further Learning


Books

Storytelling with Data - Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic
The Visual Display of Quantitative Information - Edward Tufte
Good Charts - Scott Berinato


Online

ggplot2 documentation
R Graph Gallery
Data Visualization Society

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Module 2 Overview
Previously (Module 1): - Grammar of Graphics foundations - Seven layers - Basic geoms
This Module: - Aesthetic mappings deep dive - Faceting strategies - Built-in themes - ggthemes package

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Setup: Load Data


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readxl)
library(ggthemes)  # For additional themes

# Load and prepare data
bp_data <- read_excel("../../data/PublicHealth_BP_Dataset.xlsx") %>%
  mutate(
    SysBP_Change = SysBP_6m - SysBP_0m,
    AgeGroup = cut(Age, breaks = c(0, 30, 50, 65, 100),
                   labels = c("18-30", "31-50", "51-65", "65+")),
    Hypertension_Baseline = ifelse(SysBP_0m >= 140 | DiaBP_0m >= 90, 
                                   "Hypertensive", "Normal"),
    BMI_Category = cut(BMI, breaks = c(0, 18.5, 25, 30, 100),
                       labels = c("Underweight", "Normal", "Overweight", "Obese"))
  )

# Time series data
bp_time <- bp_data %>%
  select(PatientID, TreatmentGroup, SysBP_0m, SysBP_3m, SysBP_6m) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("SysBP"),
               names_to = "Time", values_to = "SysBP") %>%
  mutate(Months = as.numeric(gsub("SysBP_|m", "", Time)))

bp_summary <- bp_time %>%
  group_by(TreatmentGroup, Months) %>%
  summarise(Mean_SysBP = mean(SysBP, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Global vs Local Aesthetics

Global aesthetics: Defined in ggplot(), apply to all layers
Local aesthetics: Defined in geom_*(), apply to specific layer
Local aesthetics override global aesthetics
Use global for shared mappings, local for layer-specific mappings



Code
ggplot(data, aes(x = var1, y = var2)) +          # Global
  geom_point(aes(color = var3)) +                 # Local (adds color)
  geom_smooth()                                   # Uses global only

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Global Aesthetics Example




Code
# Global color applies to both layers
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m, 
           color = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)



Both geom_point() and geom_smooth() use the color mapping

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Local Aesthetics Override




Code
# Local aesthetic overrides global
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = TreatmentGroup), 
             size = 3, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", 
              color = "black", linewidth = 1.5)



Points are colored by treatment, but smooth line is black

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Common Aesthetics: Color & Fill




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Region, y = SysBP_0m,
           fill = Region)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7)



color: Outlines of geoms (points, lines)
fill: Interior of geoms (bars, areas, polygons)

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Common Aesthetics: Size




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m,
           size = BMI, color = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6)



size: Point size or line width, mapped to continuous variable

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Common Aesthetics: Shape




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = Cholesterol,
           shape = Gender, 
           color = Gender)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.7)



shape: Point shape (circles, squares, triangles, etc.)
Best for categorical variables with few levels (≤6)

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Common Aesthetics: Alpha (Transparency)




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = BMI, y = SysBP_0m,
           alpha = Cholesterol)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "darkred")



alpha: Transparency (0 = transparent, 1 = opaque)
Useful for showing density in overplotted data

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Multiple Aesthetics Combined




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m,
           color = TreatmentGroup,
           shape = Gender,
           size = BMI)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6)



Can combine multiple aesthetics, but be careful not to overwhelm!

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
section: Aesthetic Mapping: Inside vs Outside aes()
text:
Aesthetic Mapping: Inside vs Outside aes()




Code
# MAPPED to data (inside aes)
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m,
           color = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_point(size = 3)

# FIXED value (outside aes)
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue", size = 3)



Key rule: Inside aes() = mapped to data, Outside = fixed value

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Common Pitfall: Mapping Constants




Code
# WRONG - Don't map constants
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m,
           color = "blue")) +        # ❌
  geom_point()

# CORRECT - Set fixed values outside aes
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue")         # ✓

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
facet_wrap(): Single Variable Faceting




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ TreatmentGroup) +
  theme_minimal()



Use for: Creating subplots for each level of one categorical variable

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
facet_wrap(): Multiple Columns




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = BMI, y = Cholesterol)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "darkred") +
  facet_wrap(~ Region, ncol = 2) +
  theme_minimal()



ncol parameter controls layout columns

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
facet_grid(): Two Variable Grid




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  facet_grid(Gender ~ TreatmentGroup) +
  theme_minimal()



Use for: Creating a grid with rows and columns from two variables
Formula: rows ~ columns

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Free Scales in Facets




Code
# Create data with different ranges
smoking_bp <- bp_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(SmokingStatus)) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(SysBP_0m, DiaBP_0m),
               names_to = "BP_Type",
               values_to = "Value")

ggplot(smoking_bp, aes(x = SmokingStatus, y = Value)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ BP_Type, scales = "free_y")



scales: “fixed” (default), “free”, “free_x”, “free_y”

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Facets with Multiple Geoms




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 1.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", 
              color = "darkred", se = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~ TreatmentGroup) +
  theme_minimal()



Each facet gets all layers - points and smooth line

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Complex Faceting Example




Code
# Handle missing data
bp_complete <- bp_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(ExerciseFreq))

ggplot(bp_complete, 
       aes(x = AgeGroup, y = SysBP_Change,
           fill = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~ ExerciseFreq, ncol = 3) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = 
          element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Theme System Overview

Themes control non-data elements of plots
Affect: fonts, colors, backgrounds, grid lines, axes
ggplot2 includes 8 built-in complete themes
Each theme suited for different contexts
Can be customized further with theme() function


Basic usage: + theme_minimal()

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
theme_gray() - Default Theme




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Region, y = SysBP_0m, 
           fill = Region)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_gray(base_size = 14)



Characteristics: Gray background, white grid lines
Best for: General exploratory analysis, default choice

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
theme_bw() - Black and White




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Region, y = SysBP_0m, 
           fill = Region)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14)



Characteristics: White background, gray grid lines, black border
Best for: Professional reports, publications, clean appearance

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
theme_minimal() - Minimalist




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Region, y = SysBP_0m, 
           fill = Region)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)



Characteristics: No background, minimal grid lines
Best for: Presentations, modern clean look, focus on data

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
theme_classic() - Classic Look




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Region, y = SysBP_0m, 
           fill = Region)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_classic(base_size = 14)



Characteristics: White background, no grid, axis lines only
Best for: Scientific publications, traditional journals, base R style

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
theme_light() & theme_dark()




Code
# Light theme
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  theme_light(base_size = 14)














Code
# Dark theme
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m)) +
  geom_point(color = "cyan") +
  theme_dark(base_size = 14)

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
theme_void() - Completely Blank




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude,
           color = Region)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.7) +
  theme_void()



Characteristics: No axes, no grid, no background
Best for: Maps, specialized graphics, pure data visualization

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text: Theme Comparison

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
ggthemes Package Overview

Additional themes inspired by famous publications and software
Professional, publication-ready aesthetics
Color palettes matching each theme
Includes themes from: Economist, FiveThirtyEight, Tufte, WSJ, Stata, Excel, and more



Code
library(ggthemes)

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
theme_economist() - The Economist Style




Code
ggplot(bp_summary, 
       aes(x = Months, y = Mean_SysBP,
           color = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) +
  scale_color_economist() +
  theme_economist()



Style: Blue background, distinctive typography
Use for: Business reports, policy documents, professional presentations

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
theme_fivethirtyeight()




Code
# Region summary
region_summary <- bp_data %>%
  group_by(Region) %>%
  summarise(Mean_SysBP = mean(SysBP_0m),
            N = n())

ggplot(region_summary, 
       aes(x = reorder(Region, -Mean_SysBP), 
           y = Mean_SysBP, fill = Region)) +
  geom_col() +
  theme_fivethirtyeight()



Style: Gray background, bold colors, large text
Use for: Data journalism, blog posts, engaging visualizations

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
theme_tufte() - Minimalism




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  theme_tufte(base_size = 14)



Style: Minimal ink, maximum data-ink ratio
Use for: Scientific papers, when “less is more”

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
theme_few() - Stephen Few’s Style




Code
ggplot(bp_data %>% filter(!is.na(BMI_Category)), 
       aes(x = BMI_Category, y = Cholesterol,
           fill = BMI_Category)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_fill_few() +
  theme_few()



Style: Clean, professional, colorblind-friendly
Use for: Business intelligence, dashboards

title: Exporting plots
text: Exporting plots from R can be done in several ways, depending on the desired output format and quality. Here are some common methods to export plots:

title: Exporting plots
text:
Using R’s Built-in Functions
R provides several built-in functions for exporting plots to different formats:

Raster Formats

png(), jpeg(), tiff(), bmp(): These functions save plots in raster formats. You can specify filename, dimensions, and resolution.

# PNG format (good for web)
png("plot.png", width = 800, height = 600, res = 100)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()

# High-resolution TIFF for publications
tiff("plot.tiff", width = 8, height = 6, units = "in", res = 300)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()


Vector Formats

pdf(): Saves plots in PDF format, vector-based and scalable.
svg(): Saves plots in SVG format, ideal for web and scalable graphics.

# PDF for high-quality prints
pdf("plot.pdf", width = 8, height = 6)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()

# SVG for web use
svg("plot.svg", width = 8, height = 6)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()

title: Exporting plots
text:
Exporting ggplot2 Plots
For ggplot2 plots, the ggsave() function is the most convenient way to export:
library(ggplot2)

# Create a plot
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point()

# Save in different formats
ggsave("plot.png", p, width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 150)
ggsave("plot.pdf", p, width = 8, height = 6)
ggsave("plot.svg", p, width = 8, height = 6)

Controlling Output Quality

Resolution (DPI): Higher DPI for print quality (300+), lower for web (72-150)
Dimensions: Specify in inches or pixels
Aspect Ratio: Maintain proportions for consistency

# High-resolution for publications
ggsave("publication_plot.tiff", p, 
       width = 6, height = 4, 
       dpi = 300, 
       device = "tiff")

# Web-optimized PNG
ggsave("web_plot.png", p, 
       width = 800, height = 600, 
       dpi = 100, 
       units = "px")

title: Exporting plots
text:
Advanced Exporting Techniques

Exporting Multiple Plots
# Save multiple plots to PDF

title: Exporting plots
text:
Best Practices

Choose the right format: PDF/SVG for vector graphics, PNG/TIFF for raster
Set appropriate resolution: 300 DPI for print, 72-150 for screen
Consider file size: Vector formats scale better but may be larger
Test outputs: Always check exported files in target applications
Use consistent dimensions: Maintain aspect ratios across exports

title: Exporting plots
text:

Plot not saving: Ensure dev.off() is called after plotting
Low quality: Increase DPI or use vector formats
Wrong dimensions: Specify units explicitly (inches, cm, pixels)
Colors not matching: Check color profiles and device settings

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
ggstatsplot is an R package that combines statistical tests and publication-ready visualisations in a single function call. Each plot automatically selects, runs, and annotates the appropriate statistical test based on your data, displaying results directly on the figure.
This removes a common workflow bottleneck: running a test in one place, building a plot in another, and manually annotating results.

install.packages("ggstatsplot")
library(ggstatsplot)

Why use it?

One function produces both the visual and the statistical result
Automatically annotates effect sizes and confidence intervals
Sensible defaults — works out of the box for most common comparisons
Output is a ggplot2 object, so you can add layers or themes as usual

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
ggbetweenstats() — Group Comparisons
Use this when you want to compare a continuous variable across two or more independent groups.

library(ggstatsplot)

# Compare systolic BP across physical-activity groups
ggbetweenstats(
  data  = ncd,
  x     = phys_act,         # grouping variable (categorical)
  y     = sbp,            # outcome variable (continuous)
  title = "Systolic BP by Physical Activity"
)








What the output shows:

A violin + boxplot combination with individual data points
The statistical test used (Welch’s ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis, chosen automatically)
The p-value, effect size (η² or ε²), and confidence interval
Pairwise comparisons (if more than 2 groups)

Choosing parametric vs non-parametric:

# Force non-parametric (Kruskal-Wallis)
ggbetweenstats(
  data  = ncd,
  x     = phys_act,
  y     = sbp,
  type  = "nonparametric"   # "parametric", "nonparametric", "robust", "bayes"
)

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
ggscatterstats() — Correlation
Use this when you want to examine the relationship between two continuous variables.

ggscatterstats(
  data  = ncd,
  x     = age,
  y     = sbp,
  title = "Age vs Systolic BP at Baseline"
)

What the output shows:

A scatter plot with a linear trend line and confidence band
Pearson (or Spearman) correlation coefficient, r
p-value and 95% confidence interval for r
Marginal histograms on both axes

Using Spearman instead of Pearson:

ggscatterstats(
  data = ncd,
  x    = age,
  y    = sbp,
  type = "nonparametric"   # uses Spearman's rho
)

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
gghistostats() — Distribution
Use this when you want to visualise the distribution of a single continuous variable with a one-sample test.

gghistostats(
  data     = ncd,
  x        = age,
  title    = "Distribution of Age",
  test.value = 40          # hypothesised population mean
)








What the output shows:

Histogram with overlaid density curve
One-sample t-test (or Wilcoxon signed-rank) against the specified test.value
Mean, median, and their confidence intervals

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
Reading the statistical annotation
Every ggstatsplot figure includes a subtitle with the test results in a standardised format:
Welch's ANOVA, F(2, 147.3) = 5.23, p = 0.006, ω² = 0.06, 95% CI [0.01, 0.14]



Component
Meaning




Test name
Which test was used (selected automatically)


Test statistic
F, t, χ², H etc.


p-value
Statistical significance


Effect size
Practical significance (ω², d, r, etc.)


95% CI
Uncertainty around the effect size









TipInterpreting effect sizes




η² / ω²: Small ≈ 0.01, Medium ≈ 0.06, Large ≈ 0.14 (for ANOVA)
Cohen’s d: Small ≈ 0.2, Medium ≈ 0.5, Large ≈ 0.8 (for t-tests)
r: Small ≈ 0.1, Medium ≈ 0.3, Large ≈ 0.5 (for correlation)

# Distribution

title: Continuous Plots - BASIC
text:
What is Continuous Data?


Definition:
Data that represents numeric measurements or quantities

Can take any value within a range
Quantitative rather than qualitative
Often derived from measurements


Examples in Our Dataset:

Age (18-79 years)
BMI (11.4-37.3)
Cholesterol levels
Blood Sugar levels
Blood Pressure (Systolic & Diastolic)
Latitude & Longitude

title: Continuous Plots - BASIC
text:
Analytical Goals for Continuous Data

What questions can we answer?

🟡 Distribution - What’s the spread? Shape? Center?
⚫ Correlation - How do two variables relate to each other?

Charts we’ll learn:

Histogram
Density Plot
Scatter Plot
Box Plot (covered in Category vs. Continuous)

# Load required libraries
library(ggplot2)    # For creating plots

# Handle missing data: select complete cases for key numeric variables
data_clean <- data %>%
  filter(!is.na(BMI), !is.na(Cholesterol), !is.na(Age))  # Remove missing values

# Preview numeric variables
summary(data_clean %>% 
  select(Age, BMI, Cholesterol, BloodSugar, SysBP_0m, DiaBP_0m))

title: Continuous Plots - BASIC
text:
Histogram - Code
🟡 Goal: Distribution (show frequency across bins)


Code
# Create histogram showing age distribution
ggplot(data_clean, aes(x = Age)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", color = "white", alpha = 0.8) +  # 30 bins
  labs(title = "Distribution of Patient Ages",
       x = "Age (years)", y = "Frequency (Number of Patients)") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +  # Serif font for professional look
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
        axis.text = element_text(size = 10))




bins = 30 divides the data into 30 equal-width intervals
Adjust bins to find optimal visualization (too few = loss of detail, too many = noise)

title: Continuous Plots - BASIC
text:
How to Read Histograms
Using the previous plot:

OBSERVATION: - Ages range from 18 to 79 years (median 50) - Patients are spread over the whole range, with somewhat more between 45 and 55 - No single sharp peak and no long tail - No gaps and no impossible values
INTERPRETATION: - The study covers the whole adult age range - No age group dominates the sample - Age is not normally distributed, but that does not matter for using it as a predictor
IMPLICATIONS: - Results can be described across adult ages - Age can be used as a continuous variable; groups (e.g. 18–39, 40–59, 60+) are only for description - Every age band has enough patients for a description
ACTIONS: - Consider age as a covariate in treatment analyses - Change bins and check the picture does not depend on it

title: Continuous Plots - BASIC
text:
Histogram with Mean/Median Lines - Code
🟡 Goal: Distribution with central tendency markers


Code
# Calculate summary statistics
age_mean <- mean(data_clean$Age, na.rm = TRUE)  # Calculate mean
age_median <- median(data_clean$Age, na.rm = TRUE)  # Calculate median

# Create histogram with reference lines
ggplot(data_clean, aes(x = Age)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", color = "white", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = age_mean), color = "red", 
             linetype = "dashed", size = 1) +  # Add mean line
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = age_median), color = "darkgreen", 
             linetype = "solid", size = 1) +  # Add median line
  annotate("text", x = age_mean + 5, y = 15, 
           label = paste("Mean =", round(age_mean, 1)), 
           color = "red", family = "serif", size = 4) +  # Label mean
  annotate("text", x = age_median - 5, y = 15, 
           label = paste("Median =", round(age_median, 1)), 
           color = "darkgreen", family = "serif", size = 4) +  # Label median
  labs(title = "Age Distribution with Mean and Median",
       x = "Age (years)", y = "Frequency") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"))

  labs(title = "Density Distribution of BMI",

  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"),

Scatter Plot - Code
⚫ Goal: Correlation between two continuous variables


Code
# Create scatter plot showing BMI vs. Cholesterol relationship
ggplot(data_clean, aes(x = BMI, y = Cholesterol)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "darkblue", size = 3) +  # Add semi-transparent points
  labs(title = "Relationship between BMI and Cholesterol",
       x = "Body Mass Index (BMI)", y = "Cholesterol (mg/dL)") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12))




alpha = 0.6 makes points semi-transparent to show overlapping
Look for patterns: positive correlation, negative, or no relationship

title: Continuous Plots - BASIC
text:
How to Read Scatter Plots
Using the previous plot:

OBSERVATION: - Points are scattered over the whole plot - No linear pattern (correlation r = 0.00, p = 0.97) - BMI ranges from 11.4 to 37.3; cholesterol from 151 to 299 mg/dL - A few BMI values below 15 sit far to the left
INTERPRETATION: - No association between BMI and cholesterol in this sample - BMI values below 15 are implausible for adults: check them before any analysis
IMPLICATIONS: - BMI alone does not predict cholesterol here - Other factors (diet, genetics, medication) are likely to matter - A scatter plot is the first data-quality check, not only a picture of association

title: Continuous Plots - BASIC

Scatter Plot with Categories - Code
⚫ Goal: Correlation + Compare groups


Code
# Scatter plot colored by Treatment Group
ggplot(data_clean, aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m, color = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 3) +  # Color points by group
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Control" = "#E74C3C", 
                                 "Intervention" = "#3498DB"),
                     name = "Treatment Group") +  # Custom colors
  labs(title = "Baseline Systolic BP by Age and Treatment Group",
       x = "Age (years)", 
       y = "Systolic Blood Pressure (mmHg)") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
        legend.position = "right")

title: Continuous Plots - BASIC
text:
Common Distribution Shapes


Normal (Bell Curve) - Symmetric around mean - Mean ≈ Median - Example: Heights
Right Skewed - Long tail to the right - Mean > Median
- Example: Income
Left Skewed - Long tail to the left - Mean < Median - Example: Age at retirement

Bimodal - Two peaks - Two distinct groups - Example: Customer segments
Uniform - Flat distribution - All values equally likely - Example: Random numbers
Outliers - Extreme values - Check for data errors - May need special handling

title: Continuous Plots - BASIC
text:
Key Takeaways

Remember:

Choose bins wisely - test different values for histograms
Density vs. Histogram - density better for comparing groups
Scatter plots reveal relationships - but don’t assume causation
Alpha transparency - helps see overlapping points
Always handle missing data - document your approach

Common Mistakes:

Too many/few histogram bins
Not handling outliers
Assuming correlation = causation
Ignoring data transformations when needed
Poor color choices for scatter plot groups

title: Time Series - BASIC
text:
What is Time Series Data?


Definition:
Data points indexed by time or ordered sequence

Observations at regular intervals
Temporal ordering matters
Shows change over time
Can reveal trends and patterns


Examples in Our Dataset:

Blood Pressure at 0, 3, 6 months
Patient measurements over time
Baseline dates
Treatment progression
Longitudinal health outcomes

title: Time Series - BASIC
text:
Analytical Goals for Time Series

What questions can we answer?

🔵 Evolution - How does it change over time?
🟡 Distribution - What’s the pattern across time periods?
🟢 Ranking - Which time period is highest/lowest?

Charts we’ll learn:

Simple Line Chart
Multiple Line Chart (comparing groups)
Line Chart with Points

title: Time Series - BASIC
text:
Setup: Load and Prepare Data


Code
# Load required libraries
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)      # For data reshaping

# Load the dataset
data <- readxl::read_excel("../../data/PublicHealth_BP_Dataset.xlsx")

# Reshape data from wide to long format for time series plotting
# Convert columns SysBP_0m, SysBP_3m, SysBP_6m to rows
bp_long <- data %>%
  select(PatientID, TreatmentGroup, SysBP_0m, SysBP_3m, SysBP_6m) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("SysBP"),
               names_to = "TimePoint",
               values_to = "SysBP") %>%  # Convert to long format
  mutate(Month = case_when(TimePoint == "SysBP_0m" ~ 0,
                           TimePoint == "SysBP_3m" ~ 3,
                           TimePoint == "SysBP_6m" ~ 6))  # Extract month number

# Preview the transformed data
head(bp_long)

title: Time Series - BASIC
text:
Simple Line Chart - Code
🔵 Goal: Show evolution over time (aggregate)


Code
# Calculate mean systolic BP at each time point
mean_bp <- bp_long %>%
  group_by(Month) %>%
  summarise(Mean_SysBP = mean(SysBP, na.rm = TRUE))  # Average across all patients

# Create line chart showing trend over time
ggplot(mean_bp, aes(x = Month, y = Mean_SysBP)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", size = 1.5) +  # Draw line
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 4) +  # Add points at each time point
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 3, 6)) +  # Show all time points on x-axis
  labs(title = "Mean Systolic Blood Pressure Over 6 Months",
       x = "Month", 
       y = "Mean Systolic BP (mmHg)") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
        axis.text = element_text(size = 10))

title: Time Series - BASIC
text:
How to Read Line Charts
Using the previous plot:

OBSERVATION: - Baseline (Month 0): mean systolic BP 135.1 mmHg - Month 3: 132.2 mmHg (2.9 mmHg lower) - Month 6: 130.4 mmHg (another 1.8 mmHg lower) - Steady downward trend, no rebound
INTERPRETATION: - Mean blood pressure fell by about 5 mmHg over six months - This line mixes both groups: it cannot say whether the intervention caused the fall
IMPLICATIONS: - Plot the groups separately (next slide): the Control mean stays at about 136 mmHg, the Intervention mean falls from 134 to 125 mmHg - An overall mean can hide that only one group changed - A change over time is not a treatment effect without a comparison group
ACTIONS: - Always show a line per group in a trial - Add error bars or confidence intervals before drawing conclusions

title: Time Series - BASIC
text:
Multiple Line Chart - Code
🔵 Goal: Compare evolution across groups


Code
# Calculate mean BP by treatment group and time
mean_bp_group <- bp_long %>%
  group_by(Month, TreatmentGroup) %>%
  summarise(Mean_SysBP = mean(SysBP, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# Create line chart with separate lines for each group
ggplot(mean_bp_group, aes(x = Month, y = Mean_SysBP, 
                          color = TreatmentGroup, group = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_line(size = 1.5) +  # Draw lines
  geom_point(size = 4) +  # Add points
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Control" = "#E74C3C", 
                                 "Intervention" = "#3498DB"),
                     name = "Treatment Group") +  # Custom colors
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 3, 6)) +
  labs(title = "Systolic BP by Treatment Group Over Time",
       x = "Month", y = "Mean Systolic BP (mmHg)") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
        legend.position = "right")

title: Time Series - BASIC
section: Line Chart with Error Bars - Code
text:
Line Chart with Error Bars - Code
🔵 Goal: Show trend with uncertainty


Code
# Calculate mean and standard error by group
bp_summary <- bp_long %>%
  group_by(Month, TreatmentGroup) %>%
  summarise(Mean_SysBP = mean(SysBP, na.rm = TRUE),
            SE = sd(SysBP, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()),  # Standard error
            .groups = "drop")

# Create line chart with error ribbons
ggplot(bp_summary, aes(x = Month, y = Mean_SysBP, 
                       color = TreatmentGroup, fill = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Mean_SysBP - SE, ymax = Mean_SysBP + SE),
              alpha = 0.2, color = NA) +  # Add confidence bands
  geom_line(size = 1.5) +  # Draw lines on top
  geom_point(size = 4) +  # Add points
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Control" = "#E74C3C", 
                                 "Intervention" = "#3498DB")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Control" = "#E74C3C", 
                                "Intervention" = "#3498DB")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 3, 6)) +
  labs(title = "Systolic BP Over Time with Standard Error",
       x = "Month", y = "Mean Systolic BP (mmHg)") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"),
        legend.position = "right")

title: Time Series - BASIC
text:
Key Time Series Concepts


Trend: - Overall direction (up, down, flat) - Long-term pattern - Calculate: moving average, regression
Seasonality: - Regular periodic fluctuations - Daily, weekly, monthly patterns - Example: Higher BP in winter
Volatility: - Amount of variation - High = unstable, Low = stable - Measure: standard deviation

Data Preparation: - Wide format: One column per time point - Long format: One row per observation - Use pivot_longer() to convert
Best Practices: - Always show all time points - Use consistent time intervals - Label axes clearly with units - Consider adding reference lines - Show confidence intervals when relevant

title: Time Series - BASIC
text:
Key Takeaways

Remember:

Connect the dots - use geom_line() to show continuity
Add points - helps identify exact time points
Multiple lines need legends - make groups clear
Show uncertainty - confidence intervals add credibility
Wide to long format - essential for time series plotting

Common Mistakes:

Not connecting points (scatter instead of line)
Too many lines (>5 becomes cluttered)
Inconsistent time intervals without noting
Missing baseline comparisons
Not handling missing time points

Lollipop Chart - Code
🟢 Goal: Ranking (cleaner alternative to bars)


Code
# Calculate counts and prepare for ordered lollipop
region_counts <- data_clean %>%
  count(Region) %>%
  arrange(n)  # Sort for proper ordering

# Create lollipop chart
ggplot(region_counts, aes(x = n, y = fct_reorder(Region, n))) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = n, y = Region, yend = Region),
               color = "gray70", size = 1.5) +  # Draw lollipop sticks
  geom_point(size = 5, color = "#2C5F8D") +  # Draw lollipop heads
  geom_text(aes(label = n), hjust = -0.5, family = "serif", size = 4) +  # Add count labels
  labs(title = "Patient Count by Region (Lollipop Chart)",
       x = "Number of Patients", y = "Region") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())  # Remove horizontal grid

title: Categorical Plots - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Reading Lollipop and Dot Plots
Using the previous plot:

OBSERVATION: - North region: widest column (33% of patients); East narrowest (20%) - Treatment share differs by region: Intervention 68% in East, 47% in North, 38% in South, 51% in West - The horizontal edges do not line up across columns - Chi-square test of Region × Treatment: p ≈ 0.05 (borderline)
INTERPRETATION: - Width of columns: regional sample sizes (North > South ≈ West > East) - Height within columns: treatment allocation within each region - Misaligned edges: allocation was not the same in every region - If this were a trial, region would need to be checked as a possible imbalance
IMPLICATIONS: - Report allocation by region, not only overall - Consider adjusting for region in the analysis - A mosaic shows this at a glance; a single overall percentage would hide it
Reading Mosaic Tips: - Misaligned tiles = association exists - Aligned tiles = independence (no association) - Area, not just height, represents proportion - Compare conditional distributions (within columns)

title: Categorical Plots - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Complex Mosaic - Code
🔴 Goal: Multi-way categorical analysis


Code
# Three-way mosaic drawn as rectangles (a mosaic is just rectangles):
# width = patients in each Gender : Treatment column, height = smoking shares
tiles <- data_clean %>%
  filter(Gender %in% c("Male", "Female")) %>%
  count(Gender, TreatmentGroup, SmokingStatus) %>%
  mutate(column = paste(Gender, TreatmentGroup, sep = " : ")) %>%
  group_by(column) %>%
  mutate(ymax = cumsum(n) / sum(n), ymin = ymax - n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup()
cols <- tiles %>% count(column, wt = n, name = "col_n") %>%
  mutate(xmax = cumsum(col_n), xmin = xmax - col_n)
tiles <- left_join(tiles, cols, by = "column")

ggplot(tiles) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax,
                fill = SmokingStatus), colour = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = (cols$xmin + cols$xmax) / 2, labels = cols$column) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Current smoker" = "#E74C3C",
                                "Former smoker" = "#F39C12",
                                "Non-smoker" = "#27AE60"),
                    name = "Smoking Status") +
  labs(title = "Smoking Status by Gender and Treatment Group",
       x = "Gender : Treatment Group (width = number of patients)", y = "Proportion") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 15, face = "bold"))

Radial Bar Chart - Code
🟢 Goal: Ranking with visual appeal (use sparingly!)


Code
# Prepare data for radial plot
exercise_counts <- data_clean %>%
  count(ExerciseFreq) %>%
  mutate(ExerciseFreq = fct_reorder(ExerciseFreq, n))

# Create radial bar chart
ggplot(exercise_counts, aes(x = ExerciseFreq, y = n, fill = ExerciseFreq)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.8, color = "white", size = 1) +  # Create bars

Key Takeaways

When to use each: - Lollipop > Bar: When you have many categories or want cleaner look - Cleveland Dot: Perfect for before/after or male/female comparisons

Raincloud Plot - Code

Purpose: Comprehensive view - combines violin + points + box
Goal: 🟡 Distribution (most complete visualization)


Code
# Create raincloud plot: Blood Pressure by Treatment Group
library(ggdist)  # For stat_halfeye

health_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(TreatmentGroup), !is.na(SysBP_6m)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = TreatmentGroup, y = SysBP_6m, fill = TreatmentGroup)) +
  # Half violin (cloud)
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5, width = 0.6, .width = 0, 
               justification = -0.2, point_colour = NA) +
  # Box plot
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5,
               position = position_nudge(x = -0.1)) +
  # Individual points (rain)
  geom_point(aes(color = TreatmentGroup), size = 1.3, alpha = 0.3,
             position = position_jitter(seed = 1, width = 0.05,
                                       height = 0)) +
  # Add mean point
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 18, 
               size = 4, color = "black") +
  coord_flip() +  # Flip to horizontal
  labs(title = "Systolic Blood Pressure at 6 Months by Treatment Group",
       subtitle = "Raincloud plot: density (cloud) + boxplot + points (rain)",
       x = "Treatment Group",
       y = "Systolic Blood Pressure (mmHg)") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme_custom() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

Enhanced Grouped Bar Chart - Code

Purpose: Compare means across two categorical variables
Goal: 🟢 Ranking + ⚫ Correlation


Code
# Calculate summary statistics
summary_data <- health_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(Gender), !is.na(ExerciseFreq), !is.na(BMI)) %>%
  group_by(Gender, ExerciseFreq) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_bmi = mean(BMI, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_bmi = sd(BMI, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(ExerciseFreq = factor(ExerciseFreq,
                              levels = c("Never", "1-2 days/week",
                                       "3-4 days/week", "5-7 days/week")))

# Create grouped bar chart with error bars and sample sizes
ggplot(summary_data, aes(x = ExerciseFreq, y = mean_bmi, fill = Gender)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(0.9), alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_bmi - se_bmi, ymax = mean_bmi + se_bmi),
                position = position_dodge(0.9), width = 0.25) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("n=", n)), 
            position = position_dodge(0.9), vjust = -1.5, size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Mean BMI by Exercise Frequency and Gender",
       subtitle = "Error bars show ± 1 SE | Numbers show sample size",
       x = "Exercise Frequency",
       y = "Mean BMI (kg/m²)",
       fill = "Gender") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Male" = "#4DBBD5", "Female" = "#E64B35")) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  theme_custom()

Common Mistakes to Avoid


Too many groups in one plot

Ignoring sample size differences

# Check missing data by group

# Load required packages

# Create custom theme
