title: Relational/Flow - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Network Diagram Basics - Code

Purpose: Show relationships between entities (nodes)
Goal: ⚫ Correlation + 🟢 Ranking


Code
# Prepare network data (patient referrals between providers)
edges <- network_data %>%
  select(from = FromProvider, to = ToProvider, 
           weight = NumReferrals) %>%
  filter(!is.na(from), !is.na(to), weight > 0)

# Create network graph object
network_graph <- graph_from_data_frame(edges, directed = TRUE)

# Calculate node importance (degree centrality)
V(network_graph)$degree <- degree(network_graph)
V(network_graph)$betweenness <- betweenness(network_graph)

# Plot network
ggraph(network_graph, layout = "fr") +  # Fruchterman-Reingold layout
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = weight, alpha = weight),
                arrow = arrow(length = unit(3, "mm")),
                end_cap = circle(3, "mm"),
                color = "gray60") +
  geom_node_point(aes(size = degree, color = degree)) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name), repel = TRUE, size = 3) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.5, 3)) +
  scale_edge_alpha(range = c(0.3, 0.8)) +
  scale_size(range = c(3, 10)) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "plasma") +
  labs(title = "Healthcare Provider Referral Network",
       subtitle = "Node size = number of connections | Arrow width = referral volume",
       size = "Connections",
       color = "Connections") +
  theme_custom()

text:
Sankey Diagram - Code

Purpose: Show flow quantities between stages
Goal: 🔴 Flow + 🔴 Part of Whole


Code
# Prepare flow data: Patient journey through treatment
# Stage 1: Initial Assessment → Stage 2: Treatment Selection → Stage 3: Outcome

# Create flow data
flow_data <- health_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(TreatmentGroup), !is.na(Adherence_Status)) %>%
  count(TreatmentGroup, Adherence_Status, name = "count") %>%
  # Rename for Sankey format
  rename(source = TreatmentGroup, target = Adherence_Status, value = count)

# Prepare nodes and links for networkD3
nodes <- data.frame(
  name = unique(c(as.character(flow_data$source), 
                 as.character(flow_data$target)))
)

# Create links with node indices
flow_data$IDsource <- match(flow_data$source, nodes$name) - 1  # 0-indexed
flow_data$IDtarget <- match(flow_data$target, nodes$name) - 1

# Create Sankey diagram
sankeyNetwork(
  Links = flow_data,
  Nodes = nodes,
  Source = "IDsource",
  Target = "IDtarget",
  Value = "value",
  NodeID = "name",
  units = "patients",
  fontSize = 14,
  nodeWidth = 30,
  sinksRight = FALSE,  # Align target nodes to left
  colourScale = JS('d3.scaleOrdinal().domain(["Treatment A", "Treatment B", "Control", "High", "Low"]).range(["#E41A1C", "#377EB8", "#4DAF4A", "#FF7F00", "#984EA3"])')
)


Note: This creates an interactive HTML widget

# Prepare data: Smoking status changes over study
alluvial_data <- health_data %>%
  select(PatientID, SmokingStatus, Gender, TreatmentGroup) %>%
  filter(!is.na(SmokingStatus), !is.na(Gender), !is.na(TreatmentGroup)) %>%
  count(TreatmentGroup, SmokingStatus, Gender)

# Create alluvial plot
ggplot(alluvial_data,
       aes(y = n, axis1 = TreatmentGroup, axis2 = SmokingStatus, 
           axis3 = Gender)) +
  geom_alluvium(aes(fill = SmokingStatus), width = 1/12, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_stratum(width = 1/12, fill = "gray90", color = "black") +
  geom_label(stat = "stratum", aes(label = after_stat(stratum)), size = 3) +
  scale_x_discrete(limits = c("Treatment", "Smoking", "Gender"),
                   expand = c(0.05, 0.05)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Never" = "#00A087", 
                              "Former" = "#3C5488",
                              "Current" = "#DC0000")) +
  labs(title = "Patient Flow: Treatment → Smoking Status → Gender",
       subtitle = "Stream width shows number of patients in each pathway",
       y = "Number of Patients",
       fill = "Smoking Status") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = "serif", size = 12),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),

Chord Diagram - Code

Purpose: Show relationships between categories in circular layout
Goal: ⚫ Correlation + 🔴 Flow


Code
# Prepare chord data: Comorbidity co-occurrence
# Simplified: Which regions refer to which treatment groups most

chord_data <- network_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(PatientRegion), !is.na(TreatmentAssigned)) %>%
  count(PatientRegion, TreatmentAssigned, name = "count") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = TreatmentAssigned, 
              values_from = count, 
              values_fill = 0)

# Convert to matrix
chord_matrix <- as.matrix(chord_data[, -1])
rownames(chord_matrix) <- chord_data$PatientRegion

# Create chord diagram
circos.clear()
circos.par(start.degree = 90, gap.degree = 4)

chordDiagram(
  chord_matrix,
  grid.col = c("North" = "#E41A1C", "South" = "#377EB8", 
               "East" = "#4DAF4A", "West" = "#984EA3",
               "Treatment A" = "#FF7F00", "Treatment B" = "#FFFF33", 
               "Control" = "#A65628"),
  transparency = 0.5,
  directional = 1,
  direction.type = c("arrows", "diffHeight"),
  diffHeight = -0.04,
  annotationTrack = "grid",
  annotationTrackHeight = c(0.05, 0.1),
  link.arr.type = "big.arrow",
  link.sort = TRUE,
  link.largest.ontop = TRUE
)

# Add labels
circos.trackPlotRegion(
  track.index = 1,
  bg.border = NA,
  panel.fun = function(x, y) {
    sector.index = get.cell.meta.data("sector.index")
    circos.text(CELL_META$xcenter, CELL_META$ylim[1], sector.index,
               facing = "clockwise", niceFacing = TRUE, adj = c(0, 0.5))
  }
)

title: Relational/Flow - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Chord Diagram - Interpretation

Reading Chord Diagrams:

Arcs represent categories

Arc width = total connections

Ribbons show connections

Ribbon width = flow strength
Color indicates source

Circular layout saves space

Shows all connections simultaneously


Our Pattern:

East region sends most patients to Treatment A
North region more balanced across treatments
West region has more Control assignments
Treatment allocation varies by region (interesting!)

When to use: Many-to-many relationships, limited space

title: Relational/Flow - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Correlation Network - Code

Purpose: Visualize correlation patterns as network
Goal: ⚫ Correlation + clustering


Code
# Calculate correlations among numeric health metrics
cor_data <- health_data %>%
  select(Age, BMI_0m, SysBP_0m, DiaBP_0m, 
         Cholesterol_0m, BloodSugar_0m) %>%
  cor(use = "complete.obs")

# Convert to network (only strong correlations)
cor_network <- cor_data %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(from = rownames(.)) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -from, names_to = "to", values_to = "correlation") %>%
  filter(from != to, abs(correlation) > 0.3) %>%  # Threshold
  mutate(abs_cor = abs(correlation))

# Create graph
cor_graph <- graph_from_data_frame(cor_network, directed = FALSE)
E(cor_graph)$weight <- cor_network$abs_cor
E(cor_graph)$cor_sign <- ifelse(cor_network$correlation > 0, "Positive", "Negative")

# Plot
ggraph(cor_graph, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = abs_cor, color = cor_sign), alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_node_point(size = 10, color = "#4DBBD5") +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name), size = 3.5, color = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(1, 4)) +
  scale_edge_color_manual(values = c("Positive" = "#00A087", "Negative" = "#DC0000")) +
  labs(title = "Health Metrics Correlation Network",
       subtitle = "Edge width = correlation strength | Color = positive/negative",
       edge_color = "Correlation",
       edge_width = "Strength") +
  theme_custom()

Interpreting Correlation Networks


Advantages:

Clusters emerge naturally

Related variables group together

Strength shown by thickness

Thicker = stronger correlation

Direction shown by color

Green = positive
Red = negative

Hub variables visible

Most connected = most important



Our Network:

SysBP & DiaBP tightly linked

Expected (measured together)

BMI cluster with BP measures

Weight affects blood pressure

Blood sugar moderately connected

Related to metabolic health

Age shows weaker connections

Less directly correlated with others

title: Relational/Flow - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Common Mistakes


Too many nodes/edges

Solution: Filter to top connections, increase threshold

Poor layout choice

Solution: Try different layouts (fr, kk, circle, tree)

Unreadable labels

Solution: Use repel = TRUE, adjust size, or interactive plots

Ignoring direction in networks

Solution: Use arrows for directed graphs

Color overload in complex diagrams

Solution: Limit to 2-3 colors, use grayscale for edges

Not showing flow magnitude clearly

Solution: Vary width, transparency, or both

text:
Interactive Networks

Benefits of Interactive Plots:


Code
library(visNetwork)

# Prepare data for interactive network
nodes_df <- data.frame(
  id = V(network_graph)$name,
  label = V(network_graph)$name,
  value = V(network_graph)$degree,  # Size by degree
  title = paste0(V(network_graph)$name, "<br>",
                "Connections: ", V(network_graph)$degree)  # Tooltip
)

edges_df <- as_data_frame(network_graph) %>%
  rename(from = from, to = to) %>%
  mutate(value = weight,  # Width by weight
         title = paste0("Referrals: ", weight))  # Tooltip

# Create interactive network
visNetwork(nodes_df, edges_df) %>%
  visOptions(highlightNearest = TRUE, nodesIdSelection = TRUE) %>%
  visPhysics(stabilization = TRUE)


Features: Hover tooltips, zoom, drag nodes, highlight neighbors

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
Note



This module builds on Quarto Basics. It assumes you can create and render a .qmd file and write basic code chunks.

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
What you will learn

Parameterised reports — run the same document for different subgroups
Inline R code — embed values directly in prose
Cross-references for figures and tables
Multiple output formats from one source file
Integrating gtsummary tables in Quarto

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
Parameterised Reports
Parameters let you run the same document with different inputs — for example, generating one report per hospital, intervention group, or region.

1. Declare parameters in the YAML header
---
title: "Site Report"
params:
  region: "North"
  group: "Control"
---


2. Use parameters in code

# params$region and params$group are available as R objects
bp <- readxl::read_excel("data/PublicHealth_BP_Dataset.xlsx")
site_data <- bp |>
  filter(Region == params$region,
         TreatmentGroup == params$group)

nrow(site_data)



3. Render with different parameter values

# Render from R for a specific site
quarto::quarto_render(
  input  = "site_report.qmd",
  output_file = "north_report.html",
  execute_params = list(
    region = "North",
    group  = "Intervention"
  )
)



4. Batch render — one file per site

library(purrr)

regions <- c("North", "South", "East", "West")

walk(regions, \(r) {
  quarto::quarto_render(
    input          = "site_report.qmd",
    output_file    = paste0(tolower(r), "_report.html"),
    execute_params = list(region = r, group = "Control")
  )
})

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
Inline R Code
Embedding computed values directly in text avoids copy-paste errors and keeps your document reproducible.
Syntax:
200

# In a code chunk (put it in a setup chunk with #| include: false in a real report):
trial    <- gtsummary::trial
n_total  <- nrow(trial)
mean_age <- round(mean(trial$age, na.rm = TRUE), 1)    # age has missing values: na.rm = TRUE
sd_age   <- round(sd(trial$age, na.rm = TRUE), 1)

In Quarto prose:
The study enrolled `r n_total` participants with a mean age of `r mean_age` years (SD = `r sd_age`).
Rendered output:

The study enrolled 200 participants with a mean age of 47.2 years (SD = 14.3).







Tip



Compute all summary values in one early code chunk marked #| include: false, then reference them via inline code throughout the document.

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
Cross-References
Cross-references auto-number figures and tables and create clickable links.

Figures
Add a label that starts with fig- and a fig-cap:
```{r}
#| label: fig-sbp-hist
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of baseline systolic blood pressure."
ggplot(bp, aes(x = SysBP_0m)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  labs(x = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", y = "Count")
```
Reference in text: @fig-sbp-hist → renders as “Figure 1”


Tables
Add a label starting with tbl- and a tbl-cap:
```{r}
#| label: tbl-demographics
#| tbl-cap: "Baseline characteristics of study participants."
library(gtsummary)
bp |>
  select(Age, Gender, SmokingStatus, Region) |>
  tbl_summary()
```
Reference in text: @tbl-demographics → renders as “Table 1”

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
Multiple Output Formats
One .qmd file can produce HTML, PDF, and Word output.
---
title: "Study Report"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    theme: flatly
  pdf:
    toc: true
    number-sections: true
  docx:
    toc: true
---
Render all formats at once:
quarto render study_report.qmd






WarningPDF requirements



PDF rendering requires a LaTeX installation. Install tinytex from R:
install.packages("tinytex")
tinytex::install_tinytex()

title: Cleaning Messy Data
text:
Real data arrive with inconsistent labels, text in number columns, duplicates and impossible values. Cleaning is not glamorous, but every later result depends on it. This page gives a checklist you can reuse, on a deliberately messy file: data/ncd_messy.csv (313 rows from a field survey).

library(tidyverse); library(janitor)
raw <- read_csv(c("../data/ncd_messy.csv", "data/ncd_messy.csv")[file.exists(c("../data/ncd_messy.csv", "data/ncd_messy.csv"))][1], show_col_types = FALSE)




Never edit the raw file. Write a script that reads it and produces a clean copy; the script is your audit trail.
Inspect before you change anything: glimpse(), summary(), count() of every categorical column, range() of every number.
Change one problem at a time and re-check after each change.
Write down what you changed and how many rows it affected.


glimpse(raw)

Rows: 313
Columns: 9
$ `Pt ID`      <dbl> 249, 288, 67, 226, 201, 132, 10, 244, 176, 1, 47, 291, 11…
$ `Age (yrs)`  <chr> "55", "48", "45", "41", "49", "45", "61", "37", "45", "42…
$ SEX          <chr> "Female", "Male", "male", "Male", "Female", "Male", "Fema…
$ Residence    <chr> "Rural", "Urban", "Rural", "Urban", "Rural", "Rural", "Ru…
$ BMI          <dbl> 24.0, 24.3, 22.1, 21.5, 25.2, 27.5, 28.3, 21.9, 23.0, 26.…
$ `Salt g/day` <chr> "11.7 g", "7.7", "8.5", "9.7", "8.4", "4.1", "10.8", "6.6…
$ SBP          <dbl> 129, 141, 125, 126, 127, 142, 147, 110, 128, 131, 134, 15…
$ Tobacco      <chr> "No", "No", "Yes", "No", "No", "No", "No", "Yes", "No", "…
$ `Visit date` <chr> "2025-01-19", "18/02/2025", "08/01/2025", "06/06/2025", "…


What the glimpse already shows: awkward names (Pt ID, Age (yrs)), Age (yrs) and Salt g/day are text (some values are not plain numbers), and 313 rows although 300 people were surveyed.




d <- raw |> clean_names()
names(d)

[1] "pt_id"      "age_yrs"    "sex"        "residence"  "bmi"       
[6] "salt_g_day" "sbp"        "tobacco"    "visit_date"


clean_names() gives lower-case names with underscores and no spaces or brackets.




count(d, sex)

# A tibble: 8 × 2
  sex        n
  <chr>  <int>
1 F         18
2 FEMALE    13
3 Female    91
4 M         22
5 MALE      13
6 Male      87
7 female    29
8 male      40


Eight spellings for two categories. Standardise, then check again:

d <- d |> mutate(sex = case_when(str_to_lower(sex) %in% c("m", "male") ~ "Male",
                                 str_to_lower(sex) %in% c("f", "female") ~ "Female"))
count(d, sex)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  sex        n
  <chr>  <int>
1 Female   151
2 Male     162

d <- d |> mutate(residence = str_trim(residence))     # "Urban " and "Urban" are different to R
count(d, residence)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  residence     n
  <chr>     <int>
1 Rural       226
2 Urban        87


case_when() returns NA for a label it does not recognise, so a surprise shows up as NA in the check. Do not hide it with a catch-all TRUE ~ ....




d |> filter(is.na(parse_number(age_yrs))) |> count(age_yrs)         # which entries are not numbers?

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  age_yrs     n
  <chr>   <int>
1 unknown     3

d <- d |> mutate(age = parse_number(age_yrs), salt_g = parse_number(salt_g_day))


as.numeric("7.2 g") gives NA; parse_number("7.2 g") reads the number and drops the unit.
Look at what turned into NA, as above, before accepting the conversion.
Dates: visit_date mixes 2025-03-14 and 14/03/2025. Parse each format separately (ymd(), dmy()) and combine, never guess.


d <- d |> mutate(visit = coalesce(ymd(visit_date, quiet = TRUE), dmy(visit_date, quiet = TRUE)))
sum(is.na(d$visit))

[1] 0






summary(d$age)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
  30.00   41.00   49.00   60.43   56.00  999.00       3 

summary(d$sbp)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
    0.0   122.0   132.0   142.7   143.0  1350.0 

d |> filter(age > 120 | sbp < 60 | sbp > 300) |> select(pt_id, age, sbp)

# A tibble: 10 × 3
   pt_id   age   sbp
   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
 1   150    48  1350
 2    99    30     0
 3    20    55  1290
 4    33   999   121
 5    69    55     0
 6    99    30     0

 8    31   999   143
 9     5   999   138
10   228   999   136



999 is a placeholder for “unknown” (check the codebook); 0 and 1350 for SBP are impossible (the second is probably 135.0 typed with a slip).
Set them to NA; do not delete the rows and do not fill in the mean:


n_bad_sbp <- sum(d$sbp < 60 | d$sbp > 300, na.rm = TRUE)     # count them before they become NA
d <- d |> mutate(age = na_if(age, 999), sbp = if_else(sbp < 60 | sbp > 300, NA_real_, sbp))
colSums(is.na(d[c("age", "sbp")]))

age sbp 
  7   6 






nrow(d)

[1] 313

nrow(distinct(d))         # exact copies of a whole row

[1] 303

d |> get_dupes(pt_id) |> select(pt_id, age, sbp, visit_date) |> head(8)

# A tibble: 8 × 4
  pt_id   age   sbp visit_date
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <chr>     
1    28    53   155 2025-01-01
2    28    53   155 2025-01-01
3    92    32   121 13/07/2025
4    92    32   121 13/07/2025
5    99    30    NA 2025-07-06
6    99    30    NA 2025-07-06
7   107    58   157 03/01/2025
8   107    58   157 03/01/2025



Exact duplicates (every column the same) are safe to remove with distinct().
The same ID with different values is not an exact duplicate: it may be a repeat visit, a re-entry or a wrong ID. Do not drop one blindly: check the source forms.





tibble(step = c("rows in raw file", "after removing exact duplicates", "age placeholders set to NA", "impossible SBP set to NA"),
       n = c(nrow(raw), nrow(distinct(raw)), sum(raw$`Age (yrs)` == "999", na.rm = TRUE), n_bad_sbp))

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  step                                n
  <chr>                           <int>
1 rows in raw file                  313
2 after removing exact duplicates   303
3 age placeholders set to NA          4
4 impossible SBP set to NA            6


Report this in the methods: it lets a reader see what was done, and lets you repeat it when a corrected file arrives.











Step
Look at
Fix with




Names
names()
clean_names()


Labels
count(col)
case_when(), fct_recode(), str_trim(), str_to_lower()


Types
glimpse(), what becomes NA
parse_number(), ymd() / dmy()


Placeholders, impossible values
summary(), range()
na_if(), if_else(), then report


Duplicates
distinct(), get_dupes()
remove exact copies; investigate repeated IDs


Record
counts before and after
a log in the script

title: Introduction to R
text:
Project: why not setwd()?

A Project (.Rproj) makes its own folder the working directory every time you open it

section: Factor levels and the reference level
text:
Factor levels and the reference level


Show the code
res <- factor(c("Urban", "Rural", "Urban"))
levels(res)        # sorted alphabetically by default: "Rural" "Urban"


[1] "Rural" "Urban"

title: Merging Datasets
text:
This module explains how to combine datasets by rows, columns, and with joins.



data1 <- data.frame(ID = 1:3, Name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"), Age = c(23, 35, 28))
data2 <- data.frame(ID = 4:6, Name = c("David", "Eva", "Frank"), Age = c(45, 30, 40))
merged_rows <- rbind(data1, data2)
merged_rows

  ID    Name Age
1  1   Alice  23
2  2     Bob  35
3  3 Charlie  28
4  4   David  45
5  5     Eva  30
6  6   Frank  40






data1 <- data.frame(ID = 1:3, Name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"))
data2 <- data.frame(Age = c(23, 35, 28), Height = c(165, 180, 175))
merged_columns <- cbind(data1, data2)
merged_columns

  ID    Name Age Height
1  1   Alice  23    165
2  2     Bob  35    180
3  3 Charlie  28    175






library(dplyr)


Attaching package: 'dplyr'


The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':

    filter, lag


The following objects are masked from 'package:base':

    intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

data1 <- data.frame(
  ID = 1:5,
  Name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "David", "Eva")
)
data2 <- data.frame(
  ID = c(2, 3, 5, 6),
  Score = c(85, 90, 88, 92)
)

inner_join(data1, data2, by = "ID")

  ID    Name Score
1  2     Bob    85
2  3 Charlie    90
3  5     Eva    88

left_join(data1, data2, by = "ID")

  ID    Name Score
1  1   Alice    NA
2  2     Bob    85
3  3 Charlie    90
4  4   David    NA
5  5     Eva    88

right_join(data1, data2, by = "ID")

  ID    Name Score
1  2     Bob    85
2  3 Charlie    90
3  5     Eva    88
4  6    <NA>    92

full_join(data1, data2, by = "ID")

  ID    Name Score
1  1   Alice    NA
2  2     Bob    85
3  3 Charlie    90
4  4   David    NA
5  5     Eva    88
6  6    <NA>    92


These join types are useful for combining medical records, survey forms, and measurement datasets.



bind_rows() (dplyr) does the same job as rbind(): tables with the same columns, different people.

library(dplyr)
round1 <- data.frame(id = 1:3, sbp = c(120, 135, 142))
round2 <- data.frame(id = 4:6, sbp = c(128, 150, 118))
bind_rows(round1, round2)

  id sbp
1  1 120
2  2 135
3  3 142
4  4 128
5  5 150
6  6 118





cbind() pastes by position and never checks who is who. If the two tables are sorted differently, the columns are silently mixed up. Join by a key such as id instead.




patients <- data.frame(id = 1:5, name = c("Asha", "Bina", "Chetan", "Dev", "Esha"))
labs     <- data.frame(id = c(3, 3, 5), hba1c = c(7.1, 6.8, 8.0))   # id 3 was tested twice
nrow(patients)

[1] 5

nrow(left_join(patients, labs, by = "id"))   # 6: patient 3 appears twice

[1] 6

count(labs, id)                                # check the key before joining

  id n
1  3 2
2  5 1


A left join keeps every patient, but a patient who matches two lab rows appears twice. Count rows before and after every join, and check that the key is unique in the table you join to.



The same blood pressures can be stored wide (one row per person, one column per measurement) or long (one row per person and measurement). ggplot2 and most models want long data.

library(tidyr)
wide <- data.frame(id = 1:3, sbp = c(128, 142, 135), dbp = c(82, 90, 85))
long <- pivot_longer(wide, cols = c(sbp, dbp), names_to = "measure", values_to = "mmHg")
long

# A tibble: 6 × 3
     id measure  mmHg
  <int> <chr>   <dbl>
1     1 sbp       128
2     1 dbp        82
3     2 sbp       142
4     2 dbp        90
5     3 sbp       135
6     3 dbp        85

pivot_wider(long, names_from = measure, values_from = mmHg)   # and back again

# A tibble: 3 × 3
     id   sbp   dbp
  <int> <dbl> <dbl>
1     1   128    82
2     2   142    90
3     3   135    85


pivot_longer() never changes the number of values: 3 people × 2 measurements = 6 rows.

title: Statistical Plots
text:
A statistical plot shows an estimate together with its uncertainty, or checks a model, instead of only the raw data. Each section below answers one question and names what to read in the plot.
library(tidyverse); library(broom); library(patchwork)
ncd <- read_csv("../data/ncd_survey.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(phys_act = factor(phys_act, levels = c("low", "moderate", "high")),
         education = factor(education, levels = c("No schooling", "Primary", "Secondary", "Graduate+")))
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))

title: Statistical Plots
text:
Categorical: proportions with confidence intervals

prev <- ncd |> filter(!is.na(education)) |> group_by(education) |>
  summarise(x = sum(htn), n = n()) |>
  mutate(p = x / n,
         lo = map2_dbl(x, n, \(x, n) prop.test(x, n)$conf.int[1]),
         hi = map2_dbl(x, n, \(x, n) prop.test(x, n)$conf.int[2]))
ggplot(prev, aes(x = education, y = p)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), colour = "#2c3e50") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("n = ", n)), y = 0.05, size = 3.5, colour = "grey40") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.6)) +
  labs(x = "Education", y = "Adults with hypertension (95% CI)", title = "A proportion is an estimate: show its CI")








prop.test() gives a confidence interval for each proportion. The smallest group (no schooling) has the widest interval: read the interval, not only the point.

title: Statistical Plots
section: Continuous: density with quantile shading, histogram with a fitted curve
text:
Continuous: density with quantile shading, histogram with a fitted curve

q <- quantile(ncd$sbp, c(0.25, 0.75))
d <- density(ncd$sbp); dd <- tibble(x = d$x, y = d$y)
p1 <- ggplot(dd, aes(x, y)) + geom_line() +
  geom_area(data = filter(dd, x >= q[1], x <= q[2]), fill = "#3498db", alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(x = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", y = "Density", title = "Middle 50% shaded")
p2 <- ggplot(ncd, aes(sbp)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 5, fill = "grey80", colour = "white") +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = mean(ncd$sbp), sd = sd(ncd$sbp)), colour = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", y = NULL, title = "Normal curve (same mean, SD)")
p1 + p2








The shaded band is the interquartile range (120 to 143 mmHg). The red curve is what a normal distribution with the same mean and SD would look like: here the data follow it closely, with a slightly longer right tail.

title: Statistical Plots
text:
Category vs category: chi-square residuals

tab <- table(ncd$phys_act, ncd$tobacco)
ct <- chisq.test(tab)
as.data.frame(ct$stdres) |> setNames(c("phys_act", "tobacco", "residual")) |>
  ggplot(aes(tobacco, phys_act, fill = residual)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", residual))) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#3498db", high = "#e74c3c", limits = c(-3, 3)) +
  labs(x = "Tobacco use", y = "Physical activity", fill = "Std. residual",
       title = sprintf("Chi-square p = %.2f: which cells drive it?", ct$p.value))








A standardised residual compares each cell with what independence predicts: beyond about ±2 the cell contributes noticeably. Here no cell comes close, matching the large p-value.

title: Statistical Plots
section: Continuous vs continuous: regression line, correlation matrix, residuals
text:
Continuous vs continuous: regression line, correlation matrix, residuals

m <- lm(sbp ~ bmi, data = ncd)
ggplot(ncd, aes(bmi, sbp)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "#e74c3c") +
  annotate("text", x = 16, y = 185, hjust = 0, size = 4,
           label = sprintf("SBP = %.0f + %.2f × BMI\nr = %.2f", coef(m)[1], coef(m)[2], cor(ncd$bmi, ncd$sbp, use = "complete.obs"))) +
  labs(x = "BMI (kg/m²)", y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", title = "The band is the CI of the mean, not of individuals")









library(ggcorrplot)
r <- cor(select(ncd, age, bmi, waist, salt_g, sbp, dbp), use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
ggcorrplot(r, type = "lower", lab = TRUE, lab_size = 3.5, colors = c("#3498db", "white", "#e74c3c"),
           title = "Pairwise correlations")








BMI and waist are almost the same measurement (r close to 1): putting both in one model causes collinearity.

a <- augment(m)
p1 <- ggplot(a, aes(.fitted, .resid)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.3) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, colour = "#e74c3c") + labs(x = "Fitted SBP", y = "Residual", title = "Residuals vs fitted")
p2 <- ggplot(a, aes(sample = .resid)) + stat_qq(alpha = 0.3) + stat_qq_line(colour = "#e74c3c") +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantile", y = "Residual quantile", title = "Normal Q-Q")
p1 + p2








A flat smooth around zero (no curve, no funnel) and points near the Q-Q line support a straight-line model with roughly normal residuals.

title: Statistical Plots
section: Visualising model output: a coefficient plot
text:
Visualising model output: a coefficient plot

m2 <- lm(sbp ~ age + sex + bmi + salt_g + tobacco + phys_act, data = ncd)
tidy(m2, conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate, y = fct_reorder(term, estimate))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), colour = "#2c3e50") +
  labs(x = "Difference in systolic BP (mmHg), 95% CI", y = NULL, title = "Adjusted coefficients")








Each row is one coefficient with its 95% CI; intervals crossing the dashed line at 0 are compatible with no difference. Note that coefficients for different units (per year, per kg/m², per category) are not comparable in size.

title: Statistical Plots
section: Category vs continuous: notched box and violin with median and IQR
text:
Category vs continuous: notched box and violin with median and IQR

tt <- t.test(sbp ~ sex, data = ncd)
p1 <- ggplot(ncd, aes(sex, sbp)) + geom_boxplot(notch = TRUE, fill = "grey85") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", title = sprintf("Welch t-test p = %.3f", tt$p.value))
p2 <- ggplot(ncd, aes(phys_act, sbp)) + geom_violin(fill = "grey90") +
  stat_summary(fun = median, fun.min = \(x) quantile(x, 0.25), fun.max = \(x) quantile(x, 0.75), colour = "#e74c3c") +
  labs(x = "Physical activity", y = NULL, title = "Median and IQR")
p1 + p2








The notch is a rough 95% interval for the median; notches that do not overlap suggest the medians differ. Print the actual test (here in the title) rather than stars.

title: Statistical Plots
Statistical Plots
section: Map: a choropleth with statistical class breaks
text:
Map: a choropleth with statistical class breaks

library(sf)
blocks <- st_read("../data/gis/district_blocks.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
br <- quantile(blocks$dengue_per_100k, probs = seq(0, 1, 0.2))
blocks$class <- cut(blocks$dengue_per_100k, breaks = br, include.lowest = TRUE, dig.lab = 3)
ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = class), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "OrRd", name = "Per 100,000\n(quintiles)") +
  labs(title = "Five classes with the same number of blocks") + theme_void()








Quintile breaks put the same number of areas in each colour; equal-interval breaks would leave most blocks in one class. State the method in the caption: the choice of breaks changes the story a map tells.

title: Regression Analysis
text: Regression models describe and quantify the relationship between an outcome and one or more predictors. This module builds up in tiers — start with a single predictor, then add predictors, then move on to diagnostics and logistic regression.
